posts.headline: PROSpect: neither prone positioning nor HFOV added ventilator-free days in early moderate-to-severe pediatric ARDS
posts.summary: In 75 PICUs in 18 countries, 424 children with early moderate-to-severe PARDS were randomised in a two-by-two factorial design to prone or supine positioning and to HFOV or conventional ventilation. The trial stopped early for futility, and ventilator-free days to day 28 did not differ for either comparison.
takeHome: Ventilator-free days did not differ: prone 17.9 vs supine 17.4 days; HFOV 17.3 vs conventional ventilation 18.0 days
Proning brought more airway plugging (rate ratio 4.83) and pressure injuries (6% vs 1%); HFOV more haemodynamic instability (rate ratio 1.84)
The authors found no evidence for prone positioning or HFOV as first-line strategies and do not recommend their routine use
authorLimitations: The trial stopped early for futility and slow enrolment after 424 of 600 planned patients
Masking was not possible given the nature of the interventions
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Prone positioning and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) are the rescue moves most PICUs reach for when a ventilated child's oxygenation worsens, yet practice varies because the pediatric data were inconclusive. Adult evidence pulls in opposite directions: proning cut mortality in severe ARDS (PROSEVA), while HFOV did not help (OSCILLATE, OSCAR).

**What they did.** This NHLBI-funded two-by-two factorial, response-adaptive trial in 75 PICUs across 18 countries enrolled patients aged 2 weeks to 20 years who had been intubated for less than 96 h before meeting moderate-to-severe PARDS criteria. Each was randomised to supine or prone and to conventional ventilation or HFOV. The primary outcome was ventilator-free days to day 28.

**What they found.**
- Enrolment stopped at 424 of 600 planned patients, for futility and slow recruitment; 168 were allocated to the HFOV arms.
- Ventilator-free days: prone 17.9 vs supine 17.4 (location shift 0.0, 95% CI -0.8 to 1.0); HFOV 17.3 vs conventional 18.0 (-0.3, -1.5 to 0.5).
- 10% had died by day 28, with no group differences.
- Proning brought more airway plugging (rate ratio 4.83) and stage 2 or worse pressure injuries (6% vs 1%); HFOV more haemodynamic instability (rate ratio 1.84).

**Caveats.** Unmasked and stopped early, but both confidence intervals exclude the 2-day gain the investigators registered as clinically meaningful.

**For the anesthesiologist.** We are often called to help prone a hypoxaemic child or move them to the oscillator. PROSpect says neither belongs as a routine first-line step in early moderate-to-severe PARDS; lung-protective conventional ventilation stays the base. If a child is proned, secure the tube and plan suctioning, since airway plugging rose almost five-fold. The registration excluded cyanotic heart disease and cardiomyopathy, so the trial does not speak to the post-bypass cardiac child.
posts.title: Prone positioning and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation in early paediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PROSpect): an international, two-by-two factorial, response-adaptive, phase 3, randomised controlled trial

options: Added about 2 ventilator-free days through day 28

posts.headline: Perioperative esketamine cut 3-month chronic pain after VATS lung resection, 14.7% vs 21.2%, in a 914-patient trial
posts.summary: In a double-blind multicentre trial in China, 914 adults having video-assisted thoracoscopic lung resection received esketamine (0.1 mg/kg at induction, 0.1 mg/kg/h during surgery, then 0.015 mg/kg/h for 48 h) or saline. The primary outcome was chronic pain at 3 months.
takeHome: Chronic pain at 3 months (NRS 1 or more on coughing): 14.7% with esketamine vs 21.2% with saline; adjusted OR 0.62 (95% CI 0.43-0.90)
A post hoc threshold of NRS 3 or more on coughing also favoured esketamine (adjusted OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.19-0.84)
Esketamine lowered pain at rest and on coughing over 48 h and reduced supplemental analgesic use, without increasing adverse effects
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Persistent pain after lung resection remains common even with thoracoscopic surgery, and few preventive strategies have been tested in large blinded trials. This one tested a simple infusion in a thoracic population large enough to look at chronic pain as the primary outcome.

**What they did.** Adults having VATS lung resection were randomised 1:1 to esketamine or saline: a 0.1 mg/kg bolus at induction, 0.1 mg/kg/h during surgery and 0.015 mg/kg/h for 48 h afterwards. The primary outcome was chronic pain at 3 months, defined as persistent pain in the surgical region scoring 1 or more on the numeric rating scale during coughing. The trial was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2000040012).

**What they found.**
- 873 of 914 randomised patients were analysed; median age 55, 63% female.
- 3-month chronic pain: 14.7% vs 21.2% (adjusted OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.43-0.90).
- With a post hoc cut-off of NRS 3 or more on coughing: adjusted OR 0.39 (0.19-0.84).
- Lower pain scores at rest and on coughing for 48 h and less supplemental analgesia through 48 h and 3 months, with no increase in adverse effects.

**Caveats.** The primary definition counts any pain on coughing, the moderate-pain analysis was post hoc, and the abstract reports outcomes only to 3 months. Intravenous esketamine is not marketed in the United States, so racemic ketamine would be the nearest substitute, and it was not what this trial tested.

**For the anesthesiologist.** For VATS lung resection, a low-dose esketamine infusion that continues for 48 h after surgery is a reasonable addition to multimodal analgesia where the drug is available. Note that the regimen ran into the postoperative period; an induction bolus alone is not what was studied.

posts.headline: NasoVISI: videolaryngoscopy beat direct laryngoscopy for infant nasotracheal intubation, 83% vs 75% first-pass success
posts.summary: Eight US pediatric cardiac centres randomised 684 infants aged 365 days or younger, without anticipated difficult airways, who needed nasotracheal intubation for elective cardiothoracic surgery or catheterisation, to videolaryngoscopy or direct laryngoscopy. The primary outcome was first-attempt success.
takeHome: First-attempt success was 83% with videolaryngoscopy vs 75% with direct laryngoscopy; adjusted risk difference 8.2% (95% CI 2.0-14.3)
Complications were similar: 13% vs 12% on the first attempt and 14% in both groups across all attempts; no cardiac arrests or deaths
The authors say the result adds to growing evidence favouring videolaryngoscopy as the first-line technique for tracheal intubation in infants
authorLimitations: Whether the benefit extends to infants with difficult airways remains an open question for further research
Whether it holds at non-specialist centres or in urgent settings is also unknown
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Many pediatric cardiac centres intubate infants through the nose because a nasal tube is easier to secure for postoperative ventilation. Videolaryngoscopy already improves first-attempt success for oral intubation in infants, but its value for nasotracheal intubation, where the tube is steered from the nose, often with Magill forceps, had not been tested. NasoVISI, funded by the APSF and the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, asked that question where nasal tubes are routine.

**What they did.** Eight US pediatric cardiac centres randomised infants aged 365 days or younger, without anticipated difficult airways, who needed nasotracheal intubation for elective cardiothoracic surgery or cardiac catheterisation, to a videolaryngoscope or standard direct laryngoscopy. First-attempt success was the primary outcome, analysed with models that accounted for clustering by intubating clinician.

**What they found.**
- 673 of 684 randomised infants were analysed; median age 14 weeks, mean weight 4.8 kg.
- First-attempt success: 83% vs 75% (adjusted risk difference 8.2%, 95% CI 2.0-14.3).
- First-attempt complications 13% vs 12%; any complication across attempts 14% in each group; no cardiac arrest or death.

**Caveats.** These were elective cases at experienced cardiac centres. The registration excluded infants under 2 kg or under 36 weeks' gestation and any infant with a known or predicted difficult airway, and the authors list difficult airways, non-specialist centres and urgent settings as open questions.

**For the anesthesiologist.** For an infant coming to the cardiac room with a planned nasal tube, starting with the videolaryngoscope gives about one extra first-pass success for every 12 infants intubated. Complications did not fall, so the gain is in first-pass success rather than proven safety. For the very small, the premature and the anticipated difficult airway, the trial offers no answer yet.
posts.title: Videolaryngoscopy versus direct laryngoscopy for nasotracheal intubation in infants undergoing cardiac procedures (NasoVISI): a multicentre, randomised controlled trial

posts.headline: HFSA: right heart failure is its own syndrome; acute care must address preload, RV afterload and contractility together
posts.summary: The Heart Failure Society of America published a scientific statement in the Journal of Cardiac Failure that frames right heart failure as a distinct clinical syndrome, with ten take-home messages on diagnosis, acute care, PAH drugs, temporary MCS and the timing of tricuspid intervention.
takeHome: Acute RHF needs all three pillars at once: optimize preload, reduce RV afterload, support contractility and perfusion, plus rhythm control and RV-protective ventilation
After LVAD or heart transplant, standardized perioperative management of preload, pulmonary vascular load, contractility and rhythm may enable earlier recognition
Temporary MCS (percutaneous or surgical RVAD, VA-ECMO) may be considered for refractory RHF with shock; choose by physiology, oxygenation needs and destination
authorLimitations: The authors list consensus definitions as a research need; reported RHF rates after LVAD or transplant depend on the definition used
Survival benefit of transcatheter tricuspid intervention remains unclear, even where symptoms and quality of life improve
They call RHF understudied and ask for standardized patient-centred endpoints, richer registries, validated prediction models and dedicated trials
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Right ventricular failure is among the hardest problems in cardiac anesthesia, off bypass, at LVAD implantation and after transplant, yet it is often treated as a by-product of left heart disease. HFSA now calls it common, prognostically important across heart failure, and a distinct clinical syndrome.

**What they did.** Corresponding author Manreet Kanwar (University of Chicago) and senior author Ryan Tedford (Medical University of South Carolina) published the statement in the Journal of Cardiac Failure on 27 October 2026, with ten take-home messages.

**What they say.**
- No single measurement defines RHF: combine examination, biomarkers and echo, adding right-heart catheterization when precision is needed.
- Acute RHF: optimize preload, reduce RV afterload and support contractility and systemic perfusion simultaneously, with rhythm management and RV-protective ventilation.
- After LVAD or transplant, standardized perioperative management of preload, pulmonary vascular load, contractility and rhythm may speed recognition and treatment.
- PAH-targeted drugs help properly classified PAH but should not be used routinely in pulmonary hypertension from left heart disease, where trials mostly showed no benefit and some agents caused edema or harm; hemodynamic phenotyping comes first.
- Temporary MCS (percutaneous RVADs, surgical RVADs, VA-ECMO) may be considered for refractory RHF with cardiogenic shock, chosen by dominant physiology, oxygenation needs and destination.
- Consider surgical or transcatheter tricuspid intervention before RV dysfunction is advanced.

**Caveats.** We read the HFSA press release, not the full statement; it gives no staging system or numeric cut-offs, and the authors list consensus definitions as a research need.

**For the anesthesiologist.** The three pillars are the levers we already pull after bypass or at LVAD implantation: volume, pulmonary vasodilation with RV-sparing ventilation, inotropes and rhythm. Judge the RV on TEE with several measures, not one number, and decide early who needs a right-sided device.
posts.title: Right Heart Failure: An HFSA Scientific Statement

quiz.question: In pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease with a failing RV, what does the HFSA right heart failure statement advise about PAH-targeted drugs?
options: Use them routinely to lower RV afterload in this group
Avoid routine use; trials mostly showed no benefit, some harm
Start them whenever echocardiography shows RV dilation
Reserve them for patients already on temporary MCS
quiz.explanation: The statement says PAH-targeted drugs help properly classified PAH but should not be used routinely in pulmonary hypertension from left heart disease, where trials mostly showed no benefit and some agents caused edema or harm; hemodynamic phenotyping comes first. Caveat: this post rests on the HFSA press release, not the full statement.

posts.headline: ESICM consensus on human-centred ICU care: flexible family visiting, structured team communication, staff support too
posts.summary: An international ESICM panel of 46 ran rapid reviews on 20 PICO questions across six domains, put 53 draft statements through a two-round eDelphi (201, then 149 stakeholders) and ratified 43 at a consensus meeting with patient and family representatives.
takeHome: Key recommendations support flexible family visitation, structured interdisciplinary communication and empathy-based training for ICU staff.
Psychological support should reach both patients and ICU professionals, together with culturally responsive care.
Environmental measures to improve sleep and reduce delirium, and integration of digital technologies, complete a 43-statement framework for diverse ICU settings.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** ICU care is no longer judged on survival alone: how families are included, how the team communicates and how staff cope all shape delirium, recovery after discharge and burnout. ESICM has now put a formal consensus behind practices that many units apply unevenly, from open visiting to structured family updates.

**What they did.** A 46-member international, multidisciplinary panel ran rapid reviews on 20 PICO questions in six domains: person-centred care; communication and transparency; emotional well-being; equity, diversity and inclusion; the ICU environment; and technology and innovation. Of 53 draft statements, a two-round eDelphi (201 participants in round 1, 149 in round 2) and a consensus meeting that included patient and family representatives endorsed 43.

**What they recommend** (from the abstract):
- Flexible family visitation
- Structured interdisciplinary communication
- Empathy-based training for staff
- Psychological support for patients and for ICU professionals
- Culturally responsive care
- Environmental measures to improve sleep and reduce delirium
- Integration of digital technologies

**Caveats.** This is a Delphi consensus built on rapid reviews rather than a graded guideline, so the statements record agreement, not proven effects on hard outcomes. We read the abstract only; the full document gives the exact wording of each statement and the level of agreement behind it.

**For the anesthesiologist.** If you staff a cardiothoracic or surgical ICU, this is an ESICM-backed reference for local policy: open visiting after cardiac surgery, a fixed structure for family updates and handovers, night-time noise and light rules as part of delirium prevention, and debriefing or psychological support for the team after hard cases.
posts.title: European Society of Intensive Care Medicine consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the intensive care unit

posts.headline: PROSPECT shoulder replacement: single-shot interscalene, paracetamol, NSAID, dexamethasone; not liposomal bupivacaine
posts.summary: A systematic review using PROSPECT methodology identified 1,809 articles, included 30 randomised trials and seven systematic reviews, and produced procedure-specific pain management recommendations for total shoulder arthroplasty.
takeHome: Basic regimen: paracetamol, an NSAID started peri-operatively and continued afterwards, IV dexamethasone 8-10 mg, and opioids only for rescue.
Regional: single-bolus interscalene block with bupivacaine or ropivacaine, not liposomal bupivacaine; local infiltration analgesia if contraindicated or expertise is lacking.
Evidence was conflicting for continuous interscalene catheters and for liposomal bupivacaine, and no evidence favoured a specific surgical technique.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Total shoulder arthroplasty causes moderate-to-severe pain, and the analgesic menu varies a lot between centres: single-shot or catheter interscalene, liposomal bupivacaine, surgeon-delivered infiltration. PROSPECT recommendations are a widely used procedure-specific reference for enhanced-recovery pathways.

**What they did.** A systematic review using PROSPECT methodology of English-language randomised trials and systematic reviews that measured postoperative pain after analgesic, anaesthetic or surgical interventions. Of 1,809 articles identified, 30 randomised trials and seven systematic reviews or meta-analyses were included, and the findings were turned into PROSPECT recommendations.

**What they recommend.**
- Paracetamol plus an NSAID given peri-operatively and continued after surgery.
- IV dexamethasone 8-10 mg.
- Single-bolus interscalene brachial plexus block with a long-acting local anaesthetic (bupivacaine or ropivacaine), not liposomal bupivacaine.
- Local infiltration analgesia when the block is contraindicated or the expertise is not available.
- Opioids for rescue only.

**Caveats.** Evidence on continuous interscalene catheters and on liposomal bupivacaine was conflicting, and the authors call for more trials of continuous infusions. The abstract does not say how diaphragm-sparing options such as superior trunk or suprascapular-based blocks were judged, so read the full paper before rebuilding a pathway around them.

**What it means for us.** The default for a shoulder arthroplasty list is simple and cheap: paracetamol, NSAID, 8-10 mg dexamethasone and a single-shot interscalene with plain bupivacaine or ropivacaine. When the interscalene is a poor choice, for example in a patient with little respiratory reserve, the recommended fallback is infiltration analgesia. Because the catheter question is still open, plan multimodal cover for the night the block wears off.

citation.title: Pain management after total shoulder arthroplasty: a systematic review and procedure‐specific postoperative pain management ( PROSPECT ) recommendations

posts.headline: FDA approves cipepofol (Cypsedo), a new IV agent for induction in adults; launch waits on DEA scheduling
posts.summary: FDA approved Haisco's Cypsedo (cipepofol) injection, 50 mg/20 mL, for induction of general anesthesia in adults undergoing surgery. The approval letter says it cannot be marketed until DEA schedules cipepofol and the label is updated.
takeHome: Approved indication: induction of general anesthesia in adults undergoing surgery; cipepofol injection 50 mg/20 mL (NDA 220482, approval letter May 29, 2026).
Marketing may begin only after DEA publishes an interim final scheduling notice for cipepofol and the labeling is revised to reflect scheduling.
Not approved in children: FDA required deferred pediatric trials, ages 3 to under 17 (report due 2028) and birth to under 3 (due 2030).
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** US anesthesiologists get a new intravenous induction agent alongside propofol, etomidate and ketamine. Cipepofol (Cypsedo, Haisco) has been reported as the first China-developed IV anesthetic approved for the US market.

**What FDA approved.** Cypsedo (cipepofol) injection, 50 mg in 20 mL (2.5 mg/mL) single-dose vials, for induction of general anesthesia in adults undergoing surgery (NDA 220482, letter signed May 29, 2026). Maintenance of anesthesia and procedural sedation are not part of the indication.

**The catch: scheduling.** The approval letter says marketing can start only after DEA publishes an interim final rule scheduling cipepofol and the label is revised to show it. Unlike propofol, it will arrive as a controlled substance, with the storage, wastage and documentation that implies.

**Label highlights.** The most common adverse reactions (2% or more) include injection-site pain and hypotension; procedural hypotension, hypertension and bradycardia are also listed. Warnings cover anaphylaxis, cardiorespiratory depression and additive hemodynamic effects with opioids and other sedatives, and patients with prior anaphylaxis to eggs, egg products, soybeans or soy products should not receive it. It is not approved in children; FDA required pediatric trials running to 2030.

**What it means for us.** Nothing changes until DEA acts. When it launches, read the label's dosing and hemodynamic data before using it in frail or cardiac patients, and decide early with pharmacy how a scheduled induction agent will be stocked and wasted.

quiz.question: FDA has approved cipepofol (Cypsedo) injection for induction of general anesthesia in adults. According to the approval letter, what must happen before it can be marketed in the US?
options: Completion of the deferred pediatric trials in children aged 3 to under 17
A post-approval study of its hemodynamic effects in frail and cardiac patients
DEA publication of an interim final scheduling notice and revision of the label to reflect it
FDA approval of the maintenance-of-anesthesia and procedural-sedation indications
quiz.explanation: The approval letter says marketing may begin only after DEA publishes an interim final rule scheduling cipepofol and the labeling is revised to show it, so unlike propofol it will arrive as a controlled substance. The deferred pediatric trials (reports due 2028 and 2030) are a post-approval requirement, not a condition of launch; maintenance and procedural sedation are not part of the indication.

posts.headline: STS borderline left heart consensus: stage LV recruitment in grey-zone neonates rather than primary biventricular repair
posts.summary: An STS panel of congenital surgeons, cardiologists and imagers used PICO questions, literature searches and a modified Delphi process to write consensus statements on borderline left heart in the first year of life, excluding unbalanced AVSD.
takeHome: Primary biventricular repair in neonates with borderline left heart should be adopted cautiously, only with favorable anatomic and physiologic criteria on echo and/or MRI.
Grey-zone neonates (small mitral and aortic valves, endocardial fibroelastosis, small LV) should undergo staged recruitment to encourage left-sided growth.
Initial palliation can be surgical Norwood or hybrid stage 1; interval catheterization and MRI should guide timing of later biventricular conversion.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters:** Whether a small left heart can carry a biventricular circulation is one of the hardest calls in congenital cardiac surgery, and practice varies widely between centers. This is the first STS expert consensus to put structure around it, and it shapes which operations (and anesthetics) these infants will need over their first year.

**What they did:** An STS panel of congenital cardiac surgeons, cardiologists and imaging experts framed key management questions with the PICO approach, searched the literature for each, and built consensus statements with a modified Delphi method. Scope: borderline left heart from the neonatal period through 1 year, excluding unbalanced atrioventricular septal defect.

**What they recommend:**
- Primary biventricular repair only for neonates with clearly favorable anatomy and physiology on echo and/or MRI.
- For the 'grey zone' (smaller mitral and aortic valves, endocardial fibroelastosis, small indexed LV diastolic volume, low ascending aortic flow): staged LV recruitment.
- Initial palliation by surgical Norwood or hybrid stage 1, possibly with atrial-level restriction; later EFE resection plus mitral and aortic valve repair as parts of complete biventricular conversion.
- Interval catheterization and MRI to time later steps.

**Caveats:** This is expert consensus built on a thin, mostly observational evidence base; the specific numeric thresholds are in the full document and were not legible in the abstract we read.

**For the anesthesiologist:** Expect more hybrid stage 1 and staged recruitment pathways, which means repeated anesthetics for catheterization and MRI in fragile single-ventricle-physiology infants, and a central role for TEE in judging mitral and aortic inflow, LV size and EFE at each surgical step.

Echo and/or MRI select neonates for primary repair, but echo alone is not the stated tool for timing conversion. This is expert consensus on a thin, mostly observational evidence base.

posts.headline: FDA Class I: BD Alaris pump infusion sets perform worse than disclosed below 1 mL/h and with boluses of 5 mL or less
posts.summary: FDA has updated its Class I recall of BD Alaris Pump Module (Model 8100) infusion sets after BD's August 2026 letter reported that sets with restrictive components perform worse than the 2025 field action disclosed. Under- or over-infusion, delayed occlusion alarms and inaccurate boluses are possible and may be hard to detect.
takeHome: Sets with closed male luers, filters, check valves, Y-sites or microbore tubing perform worse than previously disclosed.
Problems are most common at programmed rates under 1 mL/h and bolus volumes of 5 mL or less.
Discard discontinued sets, prioritize alternates for critical care, neonatal and pediatric units, or move to a syringe pump.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Alaris is the workhorse large-volume pump in many US hospitals, and this notice is about the infusions we care about most: vasopressors, inotropes and sedatives at a few tenths of a millilitre per hour, and small boluses. BD and CareFusion 303 recalled these sets in September 2025 (field action MMS-25-5311). Their August 19, 2026 letter replaces that information: updated testing found the earlier performance claims were overestimated and some sets perform significantly worse. FDA posted the updated notice on October 5, 2026 as a Class I recall.

**What is affected.** Alaris Pump Infusion Sets used with the Pump Module Model 8100 on Guardrails Suite MX software up to version 12.6, specifically sets with restrictive components: closed male luers, in-line filters, check valves, Y-sites and microbore tubing. Effects: under- or over-infusion, delayed occlusion alarms and bolus inaccuracies, mostly at rates under 1 mL/h and boluses of 5 mL or less, which users may not easily detect. Neonates, children and critically ill patients are the groups flagged. As of August 19, 2026, BD had reported no serious injuries or deaths.

**What FDA asks.** Discard the discontinued sets (Attachment C) and substitute appropriate alternates, prioritizing scarce ones for critical care, neonatal and pediatric areas; review the performance data in Attachment B; move to a syringe pump such as the Alaris Syringe Module where performance is not acceptable; otherwise use the recalled sets only with enhanced monitoring and the user-manual mitigations, including not hanging bags more than 21 inches above the pump.

**Bedside take.** Low-rate vasoactive infusions in cardiac surgical and ICU patients belong on syringe pumps with a carrier line. Ask pharmacy and biomed which set codes your ORs stock, and treat an unexplained haemodynamic swing on a low-rate Alaris infusion as a possible delivery problem before changing the dose.

quiz.question: A Class I FDA recall covers BD Alaris Pump Module (Model 8100) infusion sets with restrictive components. Under which conditions does the updated notice say under- or over-infusion and bolus inaccuracy are most likely?
options: Programmed rates above 1 mL/h with bolus volumes above 5 mL
Only on Guardrails Suite MX software versions newer than 12.6
Only with sets lacking restrictive components such as filters or check valves
Programmed rates under 1 mL/h and bolus volumes of 5 mL or less
quiz.explanation: BD's August 2026 letter reports that sets with closed male luers, filters, check valves, Y-sites or microbore tubing perform worse than previously disclosed, mostly at programmed rates under 1 mL/h and boluses of 5 mL or less, which users may not easily detect. FDA asks units to discard discontinued sets, prioritize alternates for critical care, neonatal and pediatric areas, or move to a syringe pump.

posts.headline: AHA statement maps aortic surgery from the surgeon's, anesthesiologist's and perfusionist's seats and where they collide
posts.summary: An American Heart Association scientific statement, written by cardiac surgeons and cardiac anesthesiologists, walks through the aortic surgery patient from each of the three intraoperative roles and the specific concerns each brings.
takeHome: Surgeons, anesthesiologists and perfusionists each act independently during cardiac surgery, yet one member's action can immediately affect the others.
Aortic surgery adds layers: single-lung ventilation, systemic cooling and rewarming, and myocardial, cerebral and visceral protection.
The statement presents each role's perspective to highlight specific concerns, and is explicitly not an exhaustive review of techniques.
authorLimitations: The authors state the document is not meant to be an exhaustive review of the approaches to aortic surgery.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Aortic operations are where the cardiac OR team is most interdependent: the surgeon picks the cannulation site and the perfusion strategy, the perfusionist runs cooling, rewarming and cerebral perfusion, and the anesthesiologist manages lung isolation, neuromonitoring, coagulation and TEE. A decision made in one seat changes the physiology the other two are managing, often within seconds.

**What it is.** A scientific statement from the AHA Council on Cardiovascular Surgery and Anesthesia, written by a mixed surgeon-anesthesiologist group (DeAnda, Steppan, Boskovski, Cherry, Dickey, DeAngelis, Ibekwe, Tseng). Rather than grading evidence, it takes the aortic surgery patient through the surgeon's, the anesthesiologist's and the perfusionist's perspectives and names the concerns each brings to the room.

**What it covers** (from the abstract):
- The independent but coupled actions of the three disciplines during cardiac surgery
- The extra demands of aortic work: one-lung ventilation for descending and thoracoabdominal repairs, deliberate cooling and rewarming, and protection of the heart, brain and viscera
- How each role's priorities can align or conflict

**Caveats.** This is a perspective-style statement, not a graded guideline, and the authors say up front it is not an exhaustive review of techniques. We read the abstract only; check the full text for any specific recommendations.

**For the anesthesiologist.** A useful document to hand to trainees and to bring to a team debrief or a protocol meeting. It gives you shared language for the pre-incision huddle on aortic cases: cannulation and arterial line sites, neuromonitoring plan, temperature targets and rewarming rate, the cerebral perfusion strategy, and who calls what during circulatory arrest.

posts.headline: ESC consensus gives non-transplant clinicians a playbook for heart transplant recipients, noncardiac surgery included
posts.summary: The Heart Failure Association and ACNAP of the ESC issued a clinical consensus statement on caring for heart transplant recipients outside transplant centres, covering immunosuppression, rejection, infection, late complications and situations such as noncardiac surgery.
takeHome: Better post-transplant survival means more long-term heart transplant recipients are now seen by clinicians outside specialised transplant centres.
The statement gives a structured framework: care by time since transplant, immunosuppression and drug monitoring, recognising rejection, and infection prophylaxis and treatment.
It covers noncardiac surgery, pregnancy, rehabilitation and palliative care, and stresses shared care with the centre and early referral.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Heart transplant recipients now live long enough to need hip replacements, cholecystectomies, cancer surgery and emergency trauma care, and most of that happens far from the transplant centre. The anesthesiologist covering that case is often the first clinician in days to think hard about the denervated heart, tacrolimus levels and infection risk.

**What it is.** A clinical consensus statement from the ESC's Heart Failure Association and its nursing and allied professions association (ACNAP), first author Baudry, written for non-transplant cardiologists, GPs and other clinicians with little post-transplant experience.

**What it covers** (from the abstract):
- Care principles by time since transplant
- Immunosuppressive therapy and therapeutic drug monitoring
- Recognising and managing early rejection
- Infection prophylaxis and treatment
- Surveillance for cardiac allograft vasculopathy, malignancy, chronic kidney disease and metabolic disease
- Special situations: fertility and pregnancy, noncardiac surgery, rehabilitation, palliative care
- Shared-care models and the scenarios that need early referral back to the centre

**Caveats.** Consensus, not graded evidence, and we have read only the abstract, so the specific perioperative advice still needs checking in the full text.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Worth a bookmark for the next transplant recipient on an elective list. The usual perioperative checklist applies: call the transplant team before surgery, keep immunosuppression going with minimal interruption (and check levels when absorption or drug interactions change), think about stress-dose steroids, use strict asepsis for lines, protect the kidneys, and remember the denervated heart ignores atropine, so reach for direct-acting agents such as epinephrine or isoproterenol.

posts.headline: ORACLE: supplemental OR air purification did not cut wound infections or death in 110,538 surgeries; halted for futility
posts.summary: Cluster-crossover RCT in 68 Cleveland Clinic operating rooms: each room ran an active supplemental air purification-sterilization unit or an identical sham unit in 4-week blocks, with patients, clinicians and investigators blinded. The primary outcome was a 30-day composite of surgical wound infection, infection-related complications or death after inpatient surgery.
takeHome: Primary composite after inpatient surgery: 8.1% (2,389) with active purification vs 8.2% (2,405) with sham; OR 0.98 (95% CI 0.92-1.05), P = 0.609
All surgeries (inpatient and outpatient): 5.5% vs 5.6%; OR 0.98 (0.93-1.05), P = 0.669; the futility boundary was crossed at the third interim analysis
Authors conclude supplemental active purification did not reduce wound infections or mortality; efforts may do better to focus on limiting direct wound contamination
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Surgical site infections are the most common hospital-acquired infections, and vendors sell supplemental air purification units on the premise that airborne bacteria seed wounds. Hospitals have been buying them without randomized evidence. ORACLE is that evidence.

**What they did.** Sessler and colleagues, for the ORACLE investigators, randomized 68 operating rooms in 4-week blocks to an active supplemental air purification-sterilization unit or an identical-looking sham that ran and sounded the same. Investigators, clinicians and patients were blinded. The primary outcome was a composite of surgical wound infection, infection-related complications or death within 30 days after inpatient surgery; a secondary composite added outpatients. In all, 110,538 surgeries were enrolled and 107,334 analyzed. The trial was registered as NCT04610294.

**What they found.** Nothing. The futility boundary was crossed at the third interim analysis, with 58,938 inpatients randomized. The primary composite occurred in 8.1% with active purification and 8.2% with sham (odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.05, P = 0.609). Across all surgeries it was 5.5% vs 5.6% (OR 0.98, 0.93 to 1.05, P = 0.669), with no drift over the weeks of each period.

**Caveats.** One health system with modern ventilation; the result says nothing about older rooms without HEPA filtration, or about wards and ICUs, which the authors flag as the next question. The composite blends superficial infections with deaths, and the abstract does not break out deep or implant infections.

**For anesthesiologists.** If your hospital is being pitched supplemental air sterilization for the ORs, this trial is the answer. The modifiable drivers of surgical infection remain the ones we control at the table: antibiotic timing and redosing, skin antisepsis, normothermia, glucose control and sterile technique for lines and neuraxial procedures.

posts.headline: PELICAN: keeping cardiac index at each patient's own baseline did not cut 7-day complications; 90-day death doubled
posts.summary: Multicenter European RCT of 1,111 high-risk patients having major abdominal surgery: an algorithm of crystalloid boluses and dobutamine held intraoperative cardiac index at or above the patient's preoperative resting value, versus routine hemodynamic management with the same MAP target.
takeHome: Primary composite (AKI, myocardial injury, severe infection, cardiac arrest or death within 7 days): 44.3% vs 46.9%; RR 0.94, P = .38
No between-group differences in any individual component of the primary outcome within 7 postoperative days
Authors conclude individualized cardiac index-guided therapy targeting preoperative resting cardiac index did not reduce the composite outcome versus routine therapy
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Goal-directed hemodynamic therapy has been argued over for two decades; OPTIMISE and OPTIMISE II were neutral or nearly so. The newer idea was to personalize the target: keep each patient's cardiac index at the value they had awake and resting, rather than maximizing stroke volume. PELICAN is the first large trial of that approach.

**What they did.** Saugel and colleagues randomized 1,111 patients aged 45 or older with at least one high-risk criterion having elective major visceral abdominal surgery of 90 minutes or more, at 12 university centers in five European countries (2023 to 2025). Cardiac index was measured noninvasively in everyone. The intervention arm used balanced crystalloid at 6 mL/kg/h, 500 mL boluses and dobutamine to hold cardiac index at or above the preoperative resting value; controls got usual care with the display blinded. Both arms targeted MAP above 65 mm Hg.

**What they found.** The primary composite of AKI, myocardial injury, severe infection, nonfatal cardiac arrest or death within 7 days occurred in 44.3% vs 46.9% (relative risk 0.94, 95.1% CI 0.83 to 1.08). No component differed; AKI was 9.6% vs 13.0%. The protocol worked as designed: median cardiac index 3.1 vs 2.7 L/min/m2, dobutamine in 64.1% vs 0.5%. Hospital stay was a day shorter (8 vs 9). The uncomfortable finding is 90-day mortality: 5.7% vs 2.8% (RR 2.06, 1.13 to 3.78), an exploratory secondary outcome not adjusted for multiplicity.

**Caveats.** Single-blind, one surgical population, and a mortality signal that could be chance; the trial cannot say whether dobutamine, extra fluid or something else drove it.

**For anesthesiologists.** Chasing a personalized cardiac index with routine dobutamine is not supported and may be harmful. Cardiac output monitoring remains useful for working out why a patient is hypotensive; treating the number for its own sake is not.
editorTakeHome: Composite of AKI, myocardial injury, severe infection, cardiac arrest or death at 7 days: 44.3% vs 46.9%, not different
Dobutamine ran in 64% of intervention patients versus 0.5% of controls; 90-day mortality 5.7% vs 2.8% (exploratory)
Personalized cardiac index targets with routine inotrope support should not be adopted; keep MAP above 65 and give fluid for a reason

posts.headline: Surgical bailout during TAVR fell to 0.4% of 400,000 Medicare cases, but 26% of bailed-out patients die within 30 days
posts.summary: A CMS analysis of 400,862 TAVR procedures from 2016 to 2024 finds same-day open surgery in 0.56% overall, halving over the period, with 30-day mortality of 26.3% versus 1.8% and no improvement in bailout mortality over time.
takeHome: Bailout occurred in 0.56% of 400,862 Medicare TAVRs (2016-2024); annual incidence fell from 0.92% in 2016 to 0.40% in 2024 (P<0.001)
30-day mortality after bailout was 26.3%; mortality exceeded no-bailout patients up to 1 year (P<0.001) but was similar beyond (P=0.53)
30-day mortality did not differ by hospital SAVR volume (27%, 29%, 25%; P=0.28); authors argue continued cardiac surgical support at TAVR centers is needed
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The US national coverage determination for TAVR no longer requires on-site cardiac surgery in the way it once did, and the solo TAVR operator is being argued for in print. This is the largest contemporary look at what happens when a transfemoral valve goes wrong. Braasch and colleagues published it in JACC: Cardiovascular Interventions (19:2364-2375, September 2026) with two opposing editorials.

**What they did.** Every Medicare TAVR from January 2016 to December 2024, 400,862 procedures, with surgical bailout defined as any open cardiac operation on the same day.

**What they found.**
- Bailout in 2,240 patients, 0.56% overall, falling from 0.92% in 2016 to 0.40% in 2024.
- Procedures: mediastinal hematoma evacuation 38%, ventricular repair 20%, SAVR 16%, CABG 13%, aortic surgery 11%.
- Mortality with versus without bailout: 26.3% versus 1.8% at 30 days, 35% versus 10% at one year, 48% versus 26% at five years. Early mortality did not fall over the study period. Patients who survived the first year had long-term outcomes comparable to those who never needed surgery.
- Thirty-day mortality was 41% when SAVR was combined with other interventions and 19% for isolated SAVR. Institutional SAVR volume did not change the odds: 27%, 29% and 25% across low, intermediate and high-volume centers.

**Caveats.** Administrative data cannot say why each bailout happened or how the decision was made, and a same-day operation misses rescue surgery on day two.

**For the anesthesiologist.** One in roughly 250 TAVRs still ends in an open chest, and three in four of those patients survive the first month. The editorials split on what that means for surgical standby; for the anesthesia team it means the cannulation plan, blood, and a perfusionist's phone number belong in every TAVR briefing, however routine the case looks.
editorTakeHome: Bailout fell from 0.92% in 2016 to 0.40% in 2024: hematoma evacuation 38%, ventricular repair 20%, SAVR 16%, CABG 13%, aortic 11%
Mortality after bailout 26.3% at 30 days, 35% at one year, 48% at five years, versus 1.8%, 10% and 26% without
Thirty-day death was 41% when SAVR was combined with other repairs versus 19% for isolated SAVR; institutional SAVR volume made no difference

posts.headline: MIST: multivessel CABG through a small thoracotomy beat sternotomy on 1-month physical recovery, with no deaths or strokes
posts.summary: An investigator-initiated, open-label randomised trial at seven centres in six countries assigned 170 patients with multivessel coronary disease to minimally invasive CABG via a small thoracotomy or conventional sternotomy; the primary endpoint was patient-reported physical recovery (SF-36 physical component) at one month.
takeHome: 170 patients randomised at seven centres; SF-36 physical component at 1 month 45.1 vs 42.2, mean difference 2.9 (95% CI 0.3-5.5), p=0.031.
No deaths or strokes in either group through 12 months; one early MACCE in the minimally invasive group, none with sternotomy.
Authors: in selected patients treated by experienced teams, minimally invasive CABG improved 1-month physical recovery with no apparent safety penalty through 12 months.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Minimally invasive multivessel CABG through a small left thoracotomy has spread on the promise of faster recovery, but until now the randomised evidence against sternotomy was thin. MIST is the first international randomised comparison with a patient-centred primary outcome.

**What they did.** Ruel, Nambala, Guo and colleagues randomised 170 patients with multivessel coronary artery disease 1:1 to minimally invasive CABG (86) or sternotomy CABG (84) at seven centres in six countries (NCT03447938). The trial was open-label; the primary endpoint was physical recovery at one month measured by the SF-36 physical component summary, with safety followed to 12 months. Funding came from Medtronic.

**What they found.**
- One-month SF-36 physical component: 45.1 with minimally invasive CABG versus 42.2 with sternotomy, a mean difference of 2.9 points (95% CI 0.3 to 5.5; p=0.031).
- No deaths and no strokes in either group through 12 months.
- One major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular event occurred in the minimally invasive group before one month.

**Caveats.** The trial is small, the outcome is patient-reported in an unblinded design, the centres were experienced minimally invasive programs with selected patients, and a 2.9-point SF-36 difference is modest. Long-term graft patency is not addressed here. The authors themselves call for implementation and longer-term studies.

**For the anesthesiologist.** If your surgeons take this up, the anesthetic changes more than the incision: lung isolation and one-lung ventilation during grafting, often with a double-lumen tube, TEE support for positioning and de-airing where cardiopulmonary bypass or peripheral cannulation is used, thoracotomy-appropriate analgesia (paravertebral, serratus or erector spinae blocks or catheters), and a team learning curve that the trial's experienced centres had already climbed.
editorTakeHome: SF-36 physical component at 1 month: 45.1 vs 42.2, a 2.9-point gain for minimally invasive CABG (p=0.031).
No deaths or strokes through 12 months in either arm; one early major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular event with the minimally invasive approach.
Experienced teams and selected patients; expect more one-lung ventilation, thoracotomy analgesia and peripheral cannulation in CABG rooms.

posts.headline: ESOT Bucharest consensus sets 130 rules for NRP in DCD donation: clamp, divide and vent the arch vessels
posts.summary: Thirty-one experts from nine countries reached 75% agreement on 130 statements covering when to use abdominal and thoraco-abdominal normothermic regional perfusion and how to run it; they could not agree on a maximum warm ischemia time or whether arch vessels must be transected.
takeHome: 31 experts from nine countries reached consensus on 130 NRP statements over two Delphi rounds (75% agreement threshold) to guide practice worldwide
TA-NRP brain exclusion: clamp or ligate the arch vessels, divide the cephalic ends and vent the body-side ends to atmosphere; ligation alone is insufficient
Minimum team of five roles; blood gas 3-4 minutes after start then every 30 minutes; avoid hyperoxemia, excess transfusion and cardiac distension; heart first
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** NRP is spreading faster than agreement on how to do it. The OPTN safety notice of November 2025 told US teams to transect and vent each arch vessel; this European consensus from the ESOT International DCD Congress in Bucharest is the most detailed attempt yet to write down the whole procedure. Published in Transplant International on 22 July 2026 (Minambres, first author; Cillo, corresponding), it anchors a five-paper special issue on controlled DCD.

**What they did.** Thirty-one experts from nine countries completed two Delphi rounds with 75% agreement as the threshold. Consensus landed on 130 statements.

**What they agreed.**
- Machine perfusion should be routine in cDCDD; NRP is recommended after withdrawal of life support, especially with long expected warm ischemia or a higher-risk donor.
- For TA-NRP, clamping or ligating the arch vessels plus dividing their cephalic ends and draining to atmospheric pressure excludes brain perfusion; ligation alone does not. No consensus on mandatory transection. Transcranial Doppler is not required; a written abort plan is.
- TA-NRP needs a hybrid open ECMO circuit with a rigid reservoir and a pre-withdrawal CT (or arch dissection); A-NRP needs the descending aorta clamped first. Pre-withdrawal peripheral cannulation is acceptable for TA-NRP, not A-NRP.
- Heparin and antemortem guidewires where the law allows; balanced crystalloid plus heparin in the prime; gases at 3-4 minutes then every 30; avoid hyperoxemia, transfusion excess and cardiac distension.
- Assess the heart with a PA catheter, TEE or a brief volume load. If it cannot carry the circulation, clamp the thoracic aorta and run 2.0-2.4 L/min for the abdominal organs. Order: heart, liver, lungs, then pancreas and kidneys.

**Left open.** Maximum warm ischemia time, hypoperfusion thresholds, ideal NRP duration (typically 1-2 hours) and a case number for competence.
editorTakeHome: TA-NRP brain exclusion: clamp or ligate the arch vessels, divide the cephalic ends and drain to atmosphere; ligation alone is not enough
Minimum team of five: cannulating clinician plus assistant, perfusionist, scrub and circulating nurses, coordinator; new teams work supervised
Blood gas at 3-4 minutes then every 30; avoid hyperoxemia, transfusion excess and cardiac distension; the heart comes out first
authorLimitations: No consensus on maximum warm ischemic time, the hypoperfusion threshold defining functional warm ischemia, optimal NRP duration or minimum monitoring frequency
Whether arch vessels must be transected remains a point of contention, and legal standards vary between jurisdictions
The panel was selected for NRP experience, an inherent bias that may shape its confidence on dead donor rule integrity; TA-NRP experience is limited

posts.headline: RATE: low-dose heparin or therapeutic LMWH is noninferior to standard heparin on ECMO, with no excess clotting
posts.summary: In a seven-centre Dutch open-label trial of 320 adults on VV or VA ECMO, low-dose unfractionated heparin (aPTT 1.5-2.0 times baseline) and twice-daily therapeutic LMWH were both noninferior to standard-dose heparin (aPTT 2.0-2.5 times) for a composite of severe bleeding, severe thromboembolism or death at 6 months.
takeHome: Composite of severe bleeding, severe thromboembolism or 6-month death: 81% standard-dose UFH, 72% low-dose UFH, 75% LMWH; both non-inferior
Risk differences -9.1 points (95% CI -20.3 to 2.1) for low-dose UFH and -6.1 (-17.2 to 5.0) for LMWH versus standard; margin 7.5 points
Low-dose UFH, LMWH vs standard: severe thromboembolism 10%, 9%, 11%; severe bleeding 58%, 59%, 65%; 6-month death 42%, 44%, 50%
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Bleeding is the commonest serious complication of ECMO, and most units still run heparin to an aPTT of 1.5-2.5 times baseline on habit rather than trial data. Observational series hinted that less heparin bleeds less without more clotting. RATE is the first adequately sized randomised test.

**What they did.** Seven Dutch mixed ICUs randomised 330 adults on VV (40%) or VA (60%) ECMO between 2020 and 2024 to standard-dose UFH (aPTT 2.0-2.5 times baseline, roughly 60-75 s), low-dose UFH (1.5-2.0 times, roughly 45-60 s) or weight-adjusted therapeutic LMWH twice daily. Patients with a compelling indication for full anticoagulation, known PE or intracardiac thrombus, or HIT were excluded. The primary outcome was a net composite of severe bleeding or severe thromboembolism during ECMO, or death by 6 months, with a 7.5 percentage-point noninferiority margin; 320 were analysed.

**What they found.**
- Composite: 81% standard, 72% low-dose UFH (difference -9.1%, 95% CI -20.3 to 2.1), 75% LMWH (-6.1%, -17.2 to 5.0). Both met noninferiority.
- Severe bleeding 65% vs 58% vs 59%; severe thromboembolism 11% vs 10% vs 9%.
- Six-month mortality 50% vs 42% vs 44%. Oxygenator exchanges were fewer with LMWH, and costs were lower in both intervention arms.
- Exploratory VV subgroup: mortality 23% with low-dose UFH vs 46% with standard.

**Caveats.** Open label, event rates far above the 60-70% assumed, 13-28% crossover, and anti-Xa was measured in only 71 patients. Superiority was not shown for any outcome.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** Turning heparin down to an aPTT of 1.5-2.0 times baseline, or using LMWH when renal function allows, is now the evidence-based default for most adult ECMO runs. Keep full dosing for mechanical valves, known thrombus or active PE, and stay alert for the bleeding that still hit six in ten patients.
editorTakeHome: Composite of severe bleeding, thromboembolism or 6-month death: 81% standard UFH, 72% low-dose UFH, 75% LMWH
Severe thromboembolism was 9-11% in every arm; bleeding and mortality trended lower with less anticoagulation
Lower-intensity anticoagulation is a defensible default for ECMO patients without a separate indication for full dosing

For the rest, UFH to an aPTT of 1.5-2.0 times baseline or therapeutic LMWH when renal function allows was noninferior on the composite (72% and 75% vs 81%). Open label, with 13-28% crossover.

posts.headline: Second Universal Definition of Heart Failure: rigid LVEF cut-offs dropped for reduced, preserved and improved EF
posts.summary: AHA, ACC, ESC and the World Heart Federation, with HFSA, HFA and the Japanese Heart Failure Society, updated the 2021 universal definition: HF phenotypes are grouped as reduced, preserved and improved ejection fraction without fixed numeric thresholds, a universal classification of causes is proposed, and improvement, remission and recovery trajectories are defined.
takeHome: Replaces rigid LVEF cut-offs with reduced, preserved and improved ejection fraction categories to better reflect clinical practice
Proposes a universal classification of heart failure causes and addresses HF trajectories: improvement, remission and recovery
Highlights social determinants and geographic variation in HF risk and outcomes; aims to standardize terminology for clinicians, researchers, systems and policymakers
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The 2021 universal definition gave us HFmrEF, HFimpEF and the pre-heart failure stage; every echo report, trial eligibility list and pre-op note has used that vocabulary since. The second edition, published in Circulation on 29 June 2026 and co-published in JACC (Walsh and colleagues), changes the vocabulary again.

**What they did.** A writing group convened by the AHA, ACC, ESC and World Heart Federation, in collaboration with HFSA, the HFA of the ESC and the Japanese Heart Failure Society, revised the 2021 document to standardise terminology for clinicians, researchers, health systems and policymakers and, in their words, to better reflect clinical reality.

**What changed.**
- Phenotypes move away from rigid LVEF cut-offs and are grouped as reduced, preserved and improved ejection fraction; the mildly reduced category is gone, matching the 2026 ESC heart failure guideline published in August.
- Staging keeps A (at risk), B (pre-HF), C (HF) and D (advanced HF), adds Stage 0 for people without risk factors, and sharpens the criteria for each stage.
- A universal classification of causes is proposed, grouping for example ischaemic, infective (viral, Chagas, HIV) and inflammatory (sarcoid, autoimmune, desmoplakin) cardiomyopathies, to standardise registries and trials.
- Trajectories of improvement, remission and recovery are defined, and the document addresses social determinants and geographic variation in HF risk and outcomes.

**Caveats.** A definition document, not a treatment guideline; numeric EF thresholds will persist in device and drug labels and in trial criteria for years, so expect a period of dual language.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** Update pre-operative templates and TEE reports: HFmrEF is leaving the lexicon, improved EF is a formal phenotype that still carries risk, and the cause of the cardiomyopathy should be named using the new taxonomy.
editorTakeHome: Three EF groups replace the four-tier scheme; the mildly reduced category disappears, as in the 2026 ESC guideline
Stages A to D are retained, with Stage 0 for no risk factors; pre-HF (Stage B) keeps its emphasis on prevention
A universal etiological classification (ischaemic, infective, inflammatory and others) is proposed for records and trials

This is a definition document, not a treatment guideline, so numeric EF thresholds will persist in labels and trial criteria for years.

posts.headline: ADQI/ELSO consensus on kidney support during ECMO: CRRT when medical management fails, return blood pre-oxygenator
posts.summary: The 36th ADQI meeting, held with ELSO in June 2025, produced 44 consensus statements across all ages on AKI epidemiology, fluid management, CRRT indications and delivery, biomarkers and drug dosing during ECMO (Gist and colleagues, Intensive Care Medicine, online 6 May 2026).
takeHome: AKI occurs in roughly 50-70% of ECMO patients across ages, more with VA ECMO; about half of ECMO patients receive kidney replacement therapy.
Start RRT when diuretic-based management fails patient-centred fluid or metabolic goals, usually fluid accumulation; delay may harm; ECMO itself does not mandate RRT.
Pre-pump (negative-pressure) CRRT return risks air entrainment, so use it only when other options are impractical; rapid fluid removal can harm patient and circuit.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Half of adult ECMO patients end up on CRRT, and how the filter is plumbed into the circuit, when it starts and how fast fluid comes off are decided bed by bed. This is the first joint ADQI/ELSO document.

**What they did.** The 36th ADQI consensus conference met with ELSO in June 2025 with five working groups: epidemiology and outcomes; fluid management; indications for RRT and fluid removal; CRRT delivery; and biomarkers, blood purification and pharmacokinetics. A modified Delphi required over 80% agreement (over 90% for every final statement) on 44 statements spanning neonates to adults. Recommendations are deliberately ungraded.

**Key statements.**
- Diagnose AKI by KDIGO; it occurs in 50-70% of ECMO patients and tracks with worse short- and long-term outcomes.
- Fluid accumulation is associated with harm; aim for euvolaemia with individualised, dynamic removal targets, because brisk ultrafiltration drops venous return and compromises circuit flow.
- RRT is indicated when medical management fails to meet fluid or metabolic goals and delay would be harmful; continuous modalities are preferred; no trial has tested early versus late initiation on ECMO.
- Configuration: a pre-existing dialysis catheter can run a separate circuit; otherwise an in-line haemofilter or integrated CRRT device. Return blood before the membrane lung, which traps air and clots; the negative-pressure pre-pump side is reserved for cases where nothing else is practical, with bubble sensors.
- Drug handling changes with AKI, circuit sequestration and haemodilution; use therapeutic drug monitoring more often.

**Caveats.** Opinion-based wherever trials are absent, which is most places; the statement count is reported inconsistently in the text.

**For us.** A single reference for perfusionists, intensivists and nephrologists to write one CRRT-on-ECMO protocol from, with the research agenda (timing, fluid strategy, dosing) spelled out.
editorTakeHome: AKI affects 50-70% of ECMO patients and about half receive CRRT; diagnose with KDIGO and treat modifiable risks
Start RRT when medical management fails fluid or metabolic goals, usually for fluid accumulation; ECMO itself is not an indication
Integrated CRRT returns blood before the membrane lung; avoid the pre-pump side because of air entrainment; remove fluid gradually
authorLimitations: Literature is sparse across the lifespan; many statements rest on weak or no evidence and largely on expert judgment; recommendations were intentionally not graded.
No participants from Africa or Central America, most from the United States; no patient representatives or advocacy groups took part.
Voting was not anonymous, dissenting opinions were not documented during plenary refinement, and the process was not a traditional Delphi.
Industry educational grants supported the meeting and many authors disclosed device and drug company relationships; sponsors did not take part in decisions.

posts.headline: HFA heart transplant consensus: DCD hearts now standard, machine perfusion beats cold storage, ECMO bridge fares worst
posts.summary: The Heart Failure Association's Advanced Heart Failure Committee refreshed its heart transplant consensus in the European Journal of Heart Failure: candidate thresholds, donor expansion with DCD and ex vivo perfusion, bridging strategies and management of early graft failure.
takeHome: One-year survival by bridge: ECMO 71%, percutaneous VAD 80%, temporary BiVAD 86%, temporary LVAD 90%; durable LVAD bridging does not hurt survival
Candidacy: VO2max 12 or less (14 off beta-blockers), VE/VCO2 slope over 35; PVR over 3 WU, BMI over 35, GFR under 30
Early graft failure: inotropes first, temporary MCS if severe; peripheral VA-ECMO needs LV venting; pace the atrium above 90
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Heart transplantation has changed quickly: DCD donors, ex vivo perfusion, and a waiting list where at least half the patients are bridged on a device. The HFA's Advanced Heart Failure Committee (Milicic, first author) updated its consensus in the European Journal of Heart Failure on 5 May 2026.

**Donors.** DCD hearts are called a clinical reality with excellent early outcomes, not inferior to brain-dead donors, with the potential to raise volume by about 50% where DCD donation is common. Ex vivo machine perfusion is preferred over static cold storage, and stable hypothermic preservation lowers primary graft dysfunction. Coronary angiography is advised for donors over 50 or with multiple risk factors; donors with unexplained encephalitis or unexplained arrest are excluded. A predicted heart mass ratio at or below 0.80 is linked to worse outcomes. NRP is not addressed.

**Candidates.** Contraindications are cumulative rather than absolute: persistent severe post-capillary pulmonary hypertension (PVR above 3 Wood units, tested for reversibility at catheterization), BMI above 35, GFR persistently below 30 mL/min, active substance abuse, recent cancer. Exercise thresholds: VO2max at or below 12 mL/kg/min (14 off beta-blockers) or VE/VCO2 slope above 35. PRA above 10% prompts a crossmatch.

**Bridging.** One-year survival by strategy: ECMO 71.2%, percutaneous VAD 79.9%, temporary BiVAD 86.2%, temporary LVAD 89.5%. Durable LVAD bridging gives post-transplant survival comparable to no bridge, with allosensitization screened. LVAD infection, recurrent pump thrombosis, recurrent GI bleeding, severe RV failure or refractory ventricular arrhythmia justify urgent listing; endocarditis or mediastinitis must resolve first.

**Early graft failure.** Recognize it fast, start inotropes, escalate to temporary MCS if severe. For RV failure: inotropes, inhaled nitric oxide or prostacyclin, preload optimization and atrial pacing above 90. Peripheral VA-ECMO cannot unload the LV, so add a left atrial cannula or a percutaneous VAD; VADs allow longer support.

Peripheral VA-ECMO cannot unload the LV, so a left atrial cannula or percutaneous VAD is added if it is used.

posts.headline: Vasopressin after cardiac surgery: no change in 30-day kidney events or death in 3,753 vasopressor-dependent patients
posts.summary: In a four-ICU Queensland cohort of adults needing at least six hours of vasopressors after cardiac surgery, adding vasopressin within 24 hours was not associated with major adverse kidney events at 30 days (OR 1.02) or with mortality, though the sickest tertile showed a trend toward benefit.
takeHome: Of 3,753 vasopressor-dependent post-cardiac surgery patients, 603 (16.1%) received vasopressin; 30-day MAKE not different after weighting (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.76-1.38)
No differences in 30-day mortality (OR 1.12), acute kidney injury within 7 days (OR 1.04) or new renal replacement therapy (OR 1.19)
Significant interaction with illness severity (p = 0.004), trend toward benefit in the highest-severity tertile; authors call for prospective evaluation
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Since the VANCS trial suggested vasopressin might reduce kidney injury and atrial fibrillation compared with norepinephrine in vasoplegic shock after cardiac surgery, many units reach for it early. Whether that renal benefit holds in everyday practice has been unclear.

**What they did.** Multicentre retrospective cohort from four ICUs in the Queensland Critical Care Research Network, 2015-2021. Adults admitted after CABG, valve or combined surgery who needed at least six consecutive hours of vasopressor support in the first 24 hours were included; ECMO patients were excluded. Exposure was vasopressin within 24 hours of ICU admission. Inverse probability of treatment weighting with overlap weights balanced the groups.

**What they found.**
- 3,753 patients; 603 (16.1%) received vasopressin
- Primary outcome, major adverse kidney events at 30 days (death, new renal replacement therapy or creatinine doubling): OR 1.02 (95% CI 0.76-1.38, p = 0.88)
- 30-day mortality OR 1.12 (0.69-1.82); AKI within 7 days OR 1.04 (0.85-1.28); new renal replacement therapy OR 1.19 (0.80-1.76)
- Effect modification by illness severity (interaction p = 0.004), with a trend toward benefit in the highest-severity tertile

**Caveats.** Observational, with confounding by indication that weighting can only partly address; vasopressin dose, timing relative to shock onset and catecholamine exposure were not randomised. Four ICUs in one Australian network limit generalisability, and the severity subgroup finding is hypothesis-generating.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** Use vasopressin to restore pressure and spare catecholamines when that is the problem, not as a kidney-protective strategy. The sickest-tertile signal is the question a prospective trial should answer. Print version: J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth 2026;40(7):2112-2121.
editorTakeHome: Routine vasopressin for post-bypass vasoplegia does not appear to protect the kidney; pick it for pressure, not renal rescue.
Neutral for AKI (OR 1.04), new dialysis (OR 1.19) and 30-day death (OR 1.12) after overlap weighting.
Significant interaction with illness severity (p = 0.004) keeps the door open for the sickest patients.

posts.headline: French shock guideline: norepinephrine first, dobutamine or milrinone next, Impella CP 'probably' in AMI shock
posts.summary: SRLF, the French Society of Cardiology, SFAR and the cardiac surgeons issue 41 GRADE recommendations on adult cardiogenic shock in Annals of Intensive Care, with Impella CP endorsed after a shock-team discussion in AMI shock and VA-ECMO reserved for selected deteriorating patients.
takeHome: 41 recommendations from 23 PICO questions: 7 Grade 1, 11 Grade 2, 17 expert opinion; 6 questions unanswered; all reached strong agreement
Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor with selective inotrope use; prompt treatment of the cause (culprit revascularization, urgent valve intervention) is central
Temporary MCS (Impella, VA-ECMO) reserved for carefully selected patients after shock-team discussion; structured multidisciplinary teams and regional networks underpin care
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** After DanGer Shock, ECLS-SHOCK and the 2026 ESC heart failure guideline, every country is rewriting its shock pathway. This French document, from the Societe de Reanimation de Langue Francaise and the French Society of Cardiology with SFAR and the cardiovascular surgeons, appeared in Annals of Intensive Care (16:100038) in spring 2026 with Aissaoui and Delmas as co-first authors.

**What they did.** Twenty-three PICO questions across six fields, from shock teams to de-escalation. Output: 41 recommendations, 7 Grade 1, 11 Grade 2, 17 expert opinion, 6 unanswered, all with strong agreement.

**Drugs.**
- Norepinephrine first (Grade 1+). Dopamine only when nothing else is available (1-). Epinephrine should probably not be used as vasopressor or inotrope (2-), with a last-resort caveat. Nothing on vasopressin or angiotensin II.
- Inotropes should probably be used (2+), dobutamine or milrinone first with no preference between them.

**Devices.**
- IABP: not routine in AMI shock or decompensated heart failure shock (both 1-); suggested as initial support for mechanical complications of infarction as a bridge to repair.
- Impella CP should probably be considered in AMI shock after shock-team discussion (2+), with the DanGer Shock price of more bleeding, limb ischemia and sepsis noted; Impella 5+ is suggested for predominant LV failure (expert opinion).
- VA-ECMO should probably not be used routinely in AMI shock (2-); consider it in selected deteriorating patients after shock-team discussion, and in selected bridge-to-transplant candidates. No position on MCS timing relative to PCI or on LV unloading.

**Revascularization.** Angiography as soon as feasible, culprit-lesion PCI as early as possible, non-culprit PCI staged (all 1+).

**For the anesthesiologist.** Nothing here contradicts the ESC line, which makes it a useful second reference when building a shock team: pressor and inotrope choices are explicit, and every device decision runs through the team.
editorTakeHome: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor (Grade 1+); dopamine only if nothing else exists (1-); epinephrine probably not, except as rescue
Inotropes probably yes, dobutamine or milrinone first with no preference between them; epinephrine probably not as an inotrope
IABP not routine in AMI or heart failure shock (Grade 1-), except bridging mechanical complications; Impella CP 'probably' in AMI shock

posts.headline: SOFRIB: rib plating did not shorten ICU stay and tripled pneumonia, though pain and quality of life were better later
posts.summary: In a nine-centre US trial of 236 adults with three or more displaced rib fractures plus pulmonary compromise, severe pain or deformity, surgical stabilisation within 5 days versus standardised non-operative care did not change ICU length of stay (mean difference 1.8 days, P = 0.17), lengthened hospital stay by 3.3 days and raised pneumonia from 3.3% to 11.4%, while improving SF-36 pain and physical scores.
takeHome: 236 adults with displaced rib fractures randomised to fixation within 5 days or standardised non-operative care; ICU length of stay did not differ.
Surgery meant 3.3 days longer hospital stay and more pneumonia (11.4% vs 3.3%), but better SF-36 domains and PIQ-6 impact scores.
Return to work 62.5% vs 38.7% (P=0.08); authors conclude selective rather than routine surgical stabilisation is supported.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Rib plating has spread well beyond flail chest on the strength of registry data, and the 2023 single-centre Annals trial had already shown longer hospital stays with fixation. SOFRIB is the largest multicentre randomised test, and it lands alongside the ACS chest wall injury guideline that put regional blocks on par with epidurals.

**What they did.** Ang and colleagues (Annals of Surgery, online 26 March 2026) randomised 236 adults at nine ACS-verified trauma centres between 2014 and 2024. Inclusion needed three or more displaced fractures plus pulmonary compromise, severe pain or chest wall deformity. Patients were allocated 1:1 to surgical stabilisation within 5 days (114) or standardised non-operative care (122); analysis was intention to treat and the primary outcome was ICU length of stay.

**What they found.**
- ICU stay: mean difference 1.8 days, 95% CI -0.8 to 4.4, P = 0.17.
- Hospital stay 3.3 days longer with fixation (P = 0.01); pneumonia 11.4% vs 3.3% (risk ratio 3.45, P = 0.02).
- SF-36 general health +3.3, bodily pain +4.0 and physical component +3.3 points, each beyond the minimal clinically important difference; PIQ-6 pain impact lower by 3.9 points.
- Return to work 62.5% vs 38.7%, not significant (P = 0.08).

**Caveats.** Ten years to enrol 236 patients at nine centres implies slow accrual and selection; analgesic regimens, surgical technique and timing varied; the patient-reported outcomes were secondary and unblinded.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** The acute-care case for routine plating is weaker than its advocates assumed, and the operated patient needs an anaesthetic and often a ventilator that the medically managed patient avoids. The lever you control, early catheter-based regional analgesia with aggressive pulmonary toilet, remains the standard against which fixation must prove itself. Reserve the operating room for flail segments and patients failing that care.
editorTakeHome: Primary outcome ICU length of stay: no difference; hospital stay 3.3 days longer and pneumonia 11.4% vs 3.3% with fixation
SF-36 general health, bodily pain and physical component scores improved beyond the minimal clinically important difference
Supports selective fixation for flail chest and specific patterns; blocks, catheters and respiratory therapy remain the standard

posts.headline: SVS 2026 blunt aortic injury: no repair for grades 1-2, delayed TEVAR for stable grade 3, emergent repair for grade 4
posts.summary: The Society for Vascular Surgery's focused update of its 2011 guideline (DuBose and colleagues, writing group chaired by Azizzadeh) issues 13 recommendations: definitive non-operative management for minimal aortic injury, TEVAR after 24 hours for stable grade 3 injuries so other injuries can be treated first, urgent repair when the aorta is the cause of instability, and no anti-impulse therapy for grade 1-2 injuries with traumatic brain injury.
takeHome: 13 updated recommendations replace the 2011 guideline; grades 1-2: nonoperative management, no routine follow-up imaging for grade 1, one CTA for grade 2
Grade 3 stable: delay TEVAR beyond 24 hours if other injuries need treatment; grade 3 unstable from BTAI: urgent or emergent; grade 4: emergent
Grades 1-2 with TBI: recommend against anti-impulse therapy, favor the TBI; grade 3 with TBI or solid organ injury: individualized, collaborative decisions including anticoagulation
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Blunt thoracic aortic injury is among the leading causes of death after blunt trauma, and the anaesthesiologist is the one running the blood pressure between the CT scanner and the endovascular suite. The 2011 SVS guideline predates most of the TEVAR and grading literature.

**What they did.** DuBose, Azizzadeh and the SVS writing group (Journal of Vascular Surgery, online 24 March 2026; print May 2026) commissioned a systematic review and issued 13 updated recommendations using the SVS grade 1-4 injury scale.

**What it says.**
- Grades 1 and 2 (minimal aortic injury): definitive non-operative management is recommended over TEVAR or open repair. Grade 1 needs no routine follow-up imaging; grade 2 gets a single follow-up CTA to confirm resolution.
- Grade 3, haemodynamically stable: delayed TEVAR, beyond 24 hours, is suggested so that other injuries can be addressed first.
- Grade 3 with instability attributable to the aorta: urgent (under 24 hours) or emergent intervention. Grade 4: emergent repair.
- Grade 1-2 with traumatic brain injury: anti-impulse therapy is not recommended and blood pressure management should prioritise the brain. Grade 3 with TBI or solid organ injury: anti-impulse therapy and TEVAR timing are individualised with trauma surgery and neurosurgery.
- Intraprocedural anticoagulation during TEVAR in patients with TBI or solid organ injury should be decided collaboratively.

**Caveats.** Evidence quality is low throughout and most recommendations are suggestions; left subclavian management, spinal drainage and numeric pressure targets are not covered in the summary material we could verify.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** The reflex beta-blocker infusion for every aortic injury on the CT report is gone for grades 1-2, and the patient with a concomitant head injury gets the neurosurgical pressure target. Build the heparin conversation into the pre-TEVAR huddle rather than at the moment of deployment.
editorTakeHome: Grade 1: no routine follow-up imaging; grade 2: one CTA to confirm resolution; neither gets TEVAR or open repair
Grade 3 stable: delayed TEVAR beyond 24 h; grade 3 unstable from the aorta: urgent or emergent; grade 4: emergent repair
With TBI or solid organ injury: no anti-impulse therapy for grades 1-2, individualised targets for grade 3, joint decision on heparin
