posts.headline: Pediatric Surviving Sepsis 2026: 10-20 mL/kg boluses with reassessment, peripheral pressors early, no etomidate
posts.summary: The children's Surviving Sepsis Campaign guideline is rewritten for the first time since 2020: 68 experts from 13 organizations issued 61 statements, 20 of them new, and adopted the newer organ-dysfunction definition of pediatric sepsis.
takeHome: Septic shock with ICU access: up to 40-60 mL/kg in the first hour as 10-20 mL/kg boluses, reassessing after each one
Start vasoactives through a peripheral line rather than waiting for central access; no first-line pick between epinephrine and norepinephrine
Suggests against hydrocortisone once shock responds to fluid and pressors, and against etomidate for intubation
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The adult Surviving Sepsis update landed in March 2026; this is the children's version, published online in Pediatric Critical Care Medicine on 23 March with an executive summary alongside (Weiss, first author). It comes from 68 experts across 13 organizations and adopts the newer definition of pediatric sepsis: infection plus life-threatening respiratory, cardiovascular, coagulation or neurologic dysfunction.

**What they produced.** Sixty-one statements: 5 strong recommendations, 24 conditional, 10 good-practice statements, and 22 questions with no recommendation (7 carry an 'in our practice' note). Twenty recommendations are new, 13 updated, 6 unchanged, 22 carried forward. Only three rest on high or moderate certainty.

**What they say.**
- Septic shock with ICU access: up to 40-60 mL/kg in the first hour as 10-20 mL/kg boluses, reassessing after each. Sepsis without hypotension and without ICU access: no boluses (strong, high certainty). Balanced crystalloid over saline; crystalloid over albumin.
- Vasoactives through a peripheral line rather than delaying for central access. No verdict on epinephrine versus norepinephrine, or on pressors before 40 mL/kg. At high catecholamine doses, add vasopressin or keep titrating.
- Suggests against hydrocortisone once shock is stabilized with fluid and vasoactives; stress-dose steroids still for suspected adrenal insufficiency.
- Antimicrobials within 1 hour for suspected septic shock, within 3 hours for probable sepsis without shock. Measure lactate. Cardiac and lung POCUS to guide resuscitation where skills allow; target ScvO2 of 70% or more when a central line exists.
- Suggests against etomidate for intubation; SpO2 88-92% after resuscitation; VV ECMO for refractory hypoxemia, VA ECMO only as rescue.

**For the anesthesiologist.** This is the playbook for the septic child who arrives for source control: modest boluses with reassessment, a peripheral pressor started early, no etomidate, and steroids only for adrenal insufficiency.
authorLimitations: Only three recommendations were based on high or moderate certainty of evidence; most aspects of care have relatively low quality of evidence

Give albumin rather than crystalloid boluses, reassessing after each
quiz.explanation: Sepsis without hypotension and without ICU access gets no boluses, a strong recommendation with high certainty; only three recommendations in the guideline rest on high or moderate certainty. The 10-20 mL/kg boluses with reassessment, up to 40-60 mL/kg in the first hour, apply to septic shock with ICU access, using balanced crystalloid over saline and crystalloid over albumin.

posts.headline: VATS lobectomy beats open surgery on survival in pooled randomised data: HR 0.79 for death, same disease-free survival
posts.summary: An individual patient data meta-analysis of the three randomised trials of VATS versus open lobectomy for early-stage NSCLC (Danish, Chinese and UK VIOLET; 1,185 patients) found a 21% lower hazard of death with VATS and similar disease-free survival, with no heterogeneity across trials.
takeHome: Three randomised trials, 1,185 patients (586 VATS, 599 open): overall survival favoured VATS, pooled HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.65-0.96), a 21% mortality reduction
Disease-free survival similar, pooled HR 0.91 (95% CI 0.75-1.12); no statistical heterogeneity across trials for either outcome
Authors conclude VATS improves overall survival without compromising disease-free survival and should be prioritised when technically feasible
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** VATS became the default lobectomy approach for early-stage lung cancer because patients recover faster and hurt less, not because anyone had shown it was oncologically as good. Surgeons who favoured thoracotomy pointed out that no trial was powered for survival. This NIHR-funded pooled analysis (Harris, Lim and colleagues; Lancet 2026;407:1182-1190) closes that argument.

**What they did.** A systematic search through June 2025 found three randomised trials of VATS versus open lobectomy in early-stage NSCLC: the Danish trial of Bendixen (median follow-up 9.5 years), the Chinese trial of Long (5.2 years) and the UK VIOLET trial of Lim (3.8 years). Individual patient data for all 1,185 participants (586 VATS, 599 open) were pooled in a one-stage random-effects Cox model.

**What they found.**
- Overall survival: HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.65-0.96), a 21% lower hazard of death with VATS, in the same direction in every trial.
- Disease-free survival: HR 0.91 (0.75-1.12).
- No statistical heterogeneity; excluding benign disease gave HR 0.78 for survival and 0.89 for disease-free survival.

**Caveats.** Three trials, modest total numbers, and VIOLET follow-up is still short. Because recurrence was not reduced, the survival gain presumably reflects fewer complications and better delivery of adjuvant therapy rather than a better cancer operation. Robotic approaches were not studied.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** Expect even fewer thoracotomies, and expect conversion to be a true emergency rather than a routine. The anaesthetic contribution to the survival advantage, faster extubation, less opioid and early mobilisation, is part of why minimally invasive surgery wins; the thoracotomy patient now needs the full PROSPECT analgesic package precisely because they are the exception.
editorTakeHome: Overall survival HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.65-0.96) for VATS; disease-free survival HR 0.91 (0.75-1.12)
Three trials, 586 VATS vs 599 open; result held after excluding benign disease
The oncological-equivalence worry is answered; thoracotomy now needs a technical justification

posts.headline: In 1.16 million US CABG admissions, Black patients died in hospital at 3.2% vs 2.4%; the gap did not narrow in six years
posts.summary: A National Inpatient Sample analysis of 1,159,040 isolated CABG hospitalisations found Black patients had higher in-hospital mortality (3.2% vs 2.4%, adjusted OR 1.22), two extra days in hospital and more cardiogenic shock and sepsis, with no narrowing of the gap across six years.
takeHome: National Inpatient Sample 2016-2021: 1,159,040 isolated CABG hospitalisations; Black patients were 6.7%, younger, with higher comorbidity burden.
In-hospital mortality 3.2% vs 2.4% (adjusted OR 1.22), longer stay (11.8 vs 9.6 days), more cardiogenic shock and sepsis.
No racial group showed significant improvement in mortality trends (P-trend >0.30); authors conclude disparities persist despite national initiatives.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Equity in cardiac surgical outcomes has been a stated priority of surgical and anaesthesia societies for a decade. This is the largest contemporary national look at whether anything has changed after CABG, and the answer is no.

**What they did.** Retrospective cohort using the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project National Inpatient Sample, 2016-2021. Adults undergoing isolated CABG were grouped by race and ethnicity; multivariable logistic regression adjusted for demographic and clinical factors. Primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes were length of stay, cardiac arrest, cardiogenic shock and sepsis.

**What they found.**
- 1,159,040 CABG hospitalisations; Black patients were 6.7% of cases
- Black patients were younger (mean age 63) with a higher comorbidity burden (Charlson index 3.25 vs 2.52)
- In-hospital mortality 3.2% vs 2.4% in the comparison group (adjusted OR 1.22, p < 0.01)
- Length of stay 11.8 vs 9.6 days; more cardiogenic shock and sepsis
- No significant improvement in mortality for any group over time (P-trend > 0.30)

**Caveats.** Administrative data rely on ICD coding without STS-style physiological risk variables, cannot separate hospital effects from patient effects fully, and capture only the index admission. Adjusted odds ratios describe association, not mechanism.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** The excess risk travels with comorbidity, later presentation and more shock, which are things a perioperative team can act on: anaemia and diabetes optimisation, earlier mechanical support decisions, and structured handover to the ICU. The paper is also the citation for anyone building an equity dashboard around cardiac surgical outcomes. Print version: J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth 2026;40(7):2096-2102.
editorTakeHome: Black CABG patients were younger (mean 63) but sicker (Charlson index 3.25 vs 2.52) and still died more often after adjustment.
Mortality trends were flat for every group (P-trend > 0.30): national quality programmes have not closed the gap.
Preoperative optimisation and shock recognition are the modifiable parts of this story for perioperative teams.

posts.headline: AAP policy: infants and complex children belong with fellowship-trained pediatric anesthesiologists in equipped centers
posts.summary: The AAP Section on Anesthesiology and Pain Medicine updates its policy on the critical elements of a pediatric periprocedural anesthesia environment, published in Pediatrics (March 2026), with a companion clinical report on the pediatrician's role in preparing children for anesthesia.
takeHome: Anesthesiologist privileges should reflect fellowship training and ongoing case experience; high-risk children by age, comorbidity or procedure go to designated specialists
Facilities with neonatal and pediatric ICUs should have pediatric fellowship-trained anesthesiologists; PACU needs pediatric equipment, experienced nurses, respiratory therapy and child life
Required infrastructure spans preoperative evaluation, pediatric-ready ORs, lab, blood bank and radiology, an opioid stewardship program and anesthesia QI
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Children under one year carry the highest risk of serious injury or death from anesthesia complications, and the question of which hospitals should anesthetize which children keeps surfacing in credentialing and in the ACS Children's Surgery Verification program. The AAP's Section on Anesthesiology and Pain Medicine (Long, Houck and Varughese, lead authors) has rewritten its policy, approved by the AAP board and released 23 February 2026 ahead of the March issue of Pediatrics (157:e2025075746). A companion clinical report, The Pediatrician's Role in the Evaluation and Preparation of Pediatric Patients Undergoing Anesthesia, appears in the same issue.

**What it asks for.**
- Physician anesthesiologists whose privileges reflect fellowship training and enough ongoing experience to stay competent, and advanced practice providers with appropriate pediatric training.
- Designation of high-risk patients, by age, comorbidity or procedure, to specialized anesthesiologists, with pediatric fellowship-trained anesthesiologists in facilities that run neonatal and pediatric intensive care units.
- Pediatric-specific care across the pathway: preoperative evaluation and preparation, operating rooms, laboratory, blood bank, radiology, and pediatric equipment and drugs.
- A PACU with age-appropriate equipment and experienced nursing, plus respiratory therapy and child life, and the capacity for postoperative inpatient care or a transfer partnership when complications arise.
- An acute pain program that includes opioid stewardship, and an anesthesia quality improvement program.

**Caveats.** It is a policy statement, not a graded guideline; it sets no numeric staffing ratios and names no age cut-off beyond flagging infants under one year as highest risk.

**For the anesthesiologist.** The recommendations track the ACS CSV standards closely, which is no accident given the overlap in authorship. For anyone arguing for pediatric equipment, a dedicated PACU nurse or a transfer agreement, this is the citation.

posts.headline: 2026 AHA/ACC PE guideline: 'massive' and 'submassive' are out, PERT is Class 1, deep sedation is Class 3 Harm
posts.summary: The first joint AHA/ACC clinical practice guideline on acute PE in adults, written with CHEST, SCAI, SIR and six other societies, replaces risk tiers with clinical categories A to E, makes PE response teams Class 1 for categories C to E, and warns against intubation and deep sedation unless unavoidable.
takeHome: Categories A-E are set by the most severe finding; E1 is persistent hypotension or shock, E2 refractory shock or arrest
Systemic lysis: Class 3 Harm through C2, may be considered in D, reasonable in E; VA-ECMO is the E2 alternative
If a category C-E patient must be intubated, have VA-ECMO at the bedside and use the gentlest induction you can
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Anaesthesiologists meet PE at its worst: the intraoperative collapse, the arrest on induction, the ECMO call from the cath lab. This is the first full AHA/ACC clinical practice guideline, co-written with ACCP, ACEP, CHEST, SCAI, SHM, SIR, SVM and SVN (Creager, chair; Circulation, online 19 February 2026).

**What changed.**
- Massive, submassive and low-risk are replaced by categories A (subclinical) through E (cardiopulmonary failure), assigned by the most severe indicator. C splits into C1-C3 by RV dysfunction and biomarkers, D is incipient failure such as normotensive shock, E1 is persistent hypotension or cardiogenic shock, E2 refractory shock or arrest.
- Categories C to E are admitted with troponin or BNP, lactate and echo of the RV; a PE response team is Class 1.
- Anticoagulation: DOACs over warfarin and LMWH over UFH (both Class 1); no routine IVC filters in anticoagulated patients (Class 3 Harm).
- Systemic thrombolysis is Class 3 Harm through C2, may be considered in D1-D2 and is reasonable in E. Catheter-directed lysis or mechanical thrombectomy may be considered in D and is reasonable in E1. Surgical embolectomy is reasonable in E1 but not preferred over VA-ECMO in E2.
- Deep sedation and mechanical ventilation are Class 3 Harm in categories C to E unless clinically necessary; norepinephrine is first line, dobutamine for low output, and VA-ECMO should be ready if intubation is unavoidable.

**Caveats.** Many interventional recommendations rest on registry and single-arm data; the category scheme is new and needs validation; the document covers adults only.

**For us.** Learn the letters, because consults will use them. The explicit warnings about induction and positive pressure in a failing RV, and the instruction to have ECMO available before intubating a category C-E patient, are the lines to put in your department's PE pathway.

posts.headline: International fasting consensus: encourage clear fluids until 2 h, allow 'sip til send' by protocol, gum until transfer
posts.summary: A 68-stakeholder, three-round Delphi across five continents, including patients, nurses, surgeons and anaesthetists, agreed eight recommendations: keep the 6-hour solid rule, actively encourage clear liquids until 2 hours before anaesthesia, let institutions permit more liberal intake, and resume oral intake as soon as feasible.
takeHome: Eight recommendations from 68 stakeholders over three Delphi rounds; solids 6 h (8 h after large fatty meals), non-clear liquids 6 h
Clear liquids should be encouraged until 2 h before anaesthesia or sedation; institutions may adopt protocols allowing intake within 2 h (100% agreement)
Gum and lollipops allowed until transfer; trained providers may use gastric ultrasound when more information is needed; resume oral intake as soon as feasible
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Patients routinely fast for 10-14 hours because instructions are conservative and lists slip. Prolonged fasting from clear fluids worsens thirst, hypotension at induction, glucose handling and recovery, with no evidence of fewer aspirations. National guidelines had drifted apart, and UK 'sip til send' programmes had moved ahead of them.

**What they did.** Ruggeberg and colleagues (Anaesthesia, online 9 February 2026) ran a systematic review, drafted 13 recommendations and put them through three Delphi rounds with 68 stakeholders: patients, anaesthetists, surgeons, physicians, nurses and representatives of international organisations from five continents. Eight recommendations survived.

**What they agreed.**
- Clear liquids (water, tea or coffee with a little milk, pulp-free juice, clear carbohydrate drinks) should be actively encouraged until 2 hours before the start of anaesthesia or sedation, unless an institutional protocol permits more liberal intake, such as sipping until called to the procedure room.
- Solids and non-clear liquids keep the 6-hour rule, longer after large or fatty meals; nothing solid within 2 hours.
- Salivation stimulants such as chewing gum and lollipops may continue until transfer and restart in recovery.
- Oral intake should resume as soon as clinically feasible after the procedure.
- Pre-procedural gastric ultrasound by a trained provider may inform decisions when more information is needed.

**Caveats.** Consensus, not trial evidence; adults only; it does not replace drug-specific guidance such as the multisociety advice on GLP-1 receptor agonists. Liberal regimens are meant to run inside written institutional protocols, not ad hoc.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** The direction of travel is settled: the default is a drink two hours before, not nil by mouth from midnight. Writing the local protocol, including who decides on the delayed case and when to scan the stomach, is now the job.
editorTakeHome: Clear liquids should be encouraged, not merely permitted, until 2 h before anaesthesia or sedation
Institutions may adopt more liberal protocols such as sipping until called; solids stay at 6 h, longer for heavy meals
Chewing gum and sweets allowed until transfer; a trained operator's gastric ultrasound can settle doubtful cases
authorLimitations: Evidence underpinning the recommendations is very limited
Panel selection, partly by literature search and partly via international organisations, could appear arbitrary
Not all stakeholders could attend the online final Delphi round; every recommendation had already reached agreement in two earlier rounds
The statement carries no endorsement from any organisation or society

posts.headline: ASE/EACVI strain consensus endorses GLS, RV free-wall and LA reservoir strain; radial and regional strain are not
posts.summary: The first joint ASE/EACVI document devoted to clinical strain (Thomas, chair), published in JASE in November 2025 and in EHJ-Cardiovascular Imaging on 30 January 2026, grades every strain measure by indication and standardizes acquisition and reporting.
takeHome: LV GLS endorsed for cardio-oncology and valve-disease prognosis; report end-systolic strain with the negative sign and quote vendor-specific normals
RV free-wall strain endorsed in MI, heart failure, cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension; use the RV-focused apical view and dedicated RV software
Radial strain and regional strain are not endorsed; no randomized trial has tested strain-guided decisions, so the grades are expert opinion
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Strain has lived in guidelines piecemeal since 2015, with vendors, views and cut-offs that never quite lined up. This is the first joint ASE/EACVI document devoted to its clinical use, published in JASE in November 2025 and in European Heart Journal - Cardiovascular Imaging (27:335-368) on 30 January 2026.

**What they did.** The writing group graded each measure, by indication, as clinically endorsed (+++), may be appropriate (++), or not currently endorsed, and set out technical standards and pitfalls. No large randomized trial has tested strain-based decisions, so the grades are expert opinion.

**What is endorsed.**
- LV GLS as a complementary measure of global function, reported as end-systolic longitudinal strain with the negative sign kept; lower limits of normal differ slightly by vendor. It gets +++ for diagnosis and prognosis in cardio-oncology and for prognosis in at least moderate valve disease.
- RV free-wall longitudinal strain is +++ for diagnosis and prognosis in acute and chronic MI, heart failure, undifferentiated cardiomyopathy, CRT, athlete's heart and pulmonary hypertension, and ++ in adult congenital disease and stress echo. Use the RV-focused apical four-chamber view, because the standard view underestimates, and dedicated RV software rather than repurposed LV software.
- LA reservoir strain is +++ in undifferentiated cardiomyopathy and acute and chronic heart failure, ++ in most other settings, and not endorsed in adult congenital disease.

**What is not.** Radial strain is not endorsed. Regional strain is not supported because of variability, though curve shape can help. Midwall or full-wall tracking is preferred; speckle tracking for chamber-wide assessment, tissue Doppler for a single region.

**For the perioperative echo reader.** RV free-wall strain and GLS now carry society backing for the RV-failure and valve-disease questions that precede LVAD and valve surgery, provided you use the right view and software.

posts.headline: SCA and STS publish the first joint consensus on managing DOACs before, during and after cardiac surgery
posts.summary: The Society of Cardiovascular Anesthesiologists and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons issued a joint consensus statement on patients taking factor Xa or direct thrombin inhibitors who need cardiac surgery, built on a systematic review plus expert consensus, published in Anesthesia & Analgesia (online 29 January 2026, April 2026 issue) and co-published in the Annals of Thoracic Surgery.
takeHome: Five domains: when to stop the DOAC, how to check residual drug activity, whether to bridge, how to reverse, when to restart.
Summary statements pair the evidence with expert consensus for each domain, written for anesthesiologists and surgeons together.
Use it to rebuild your pre-admission DOAC protocol, assay access and emergency reversal pathway; read the full text for specifics.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** A large share of patients arriving for CABG, valve or aortic surgery are on apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban or dabigatran, and the questions come up every week: how many days to hold, whether a drug level is worth sending, what to do when surgery cannot wait, which reversal agent to reach for, and when the surgeon is comfortable restarting. Practice has varied by institution and by who was on call. European surgeons issued recommendations in 2023; this is the first joint statement from the two US societies that share these patients.

**What they did.** Budd, Kertai, Wyler von Ballmoos, Raphael, Ghadimi and colleagues, writing for the SCA and the STS, ran a systematic review of the literature on stopping DOACs before cardiac surgery, monitoring options, the need for bridging, reversal agents, and resuming anticoagulation after surgery, then completed a structured expert consensus process. The output is a set of summary statements for each domain, each tied to the evidence and the panel's agreement.

**What it covers.**
- Preoperative cessation, including how renal function and drug choice change the timing.
- Measuring residual effect, and where calibrated assays help when timing is uncertain or surgery is urgent.
- Bridging, which the statement addresses directly rather than leaving to habit.
- Reversal strategies for emergent and bleeding patients, including the specific reversal agents and prothrombin complex concentrate.
- Postoperative resumption in a way both specialties can sign off on.

**Caveats.** Much of the base is observational, so several statements rest on consensus rather than trial data, and the document is a guide rather than an hour-by-hour mandate; the full text carries the specifics this summary deliberately does not paraphrase.

**For the anesthesiologist.** This is the document to cite when you standardize the DOAC questions in pre-admission testing, secure anti-Xa and dabigatran assays with a quick turnaround, agree a reversal pathway with pharmacy and blood bank, and set a resumption plan with your surgeons.

posts.headline: Association of Anaesthetists/BIHS 2026: proceed with elective surgery below 180/120 in clinic; home readings now count
posts.summary: The planned update of the 2016 UK blood pressure guideline, built by Delphi, tells hospitals to accept referrals with a documented clinic BP under 160/100 (or home or ambulatory under 155/95) in the past year, and to proceed at pre-assessment if the clinic reading is under 180/120 or the out-of-office reading under 175/115.
takeHome: Secondary care peri-operative teams should accept referrals documenting clinic BP <160/100 mmHg or ambulatory/home BP <155/95 mmHg within 12 months
Without primary care documentation of normotension, patients may proceed to elective surgery if clinic BP <180/120 mmHg or ambulatory/home <175/115 mmHg
Covers decision to operate until 30 days after planned surgery in adults (excluding cardiothoracic, obstetric, endocrine); targeted review plus modified Delphi
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** A raised blood pressure on the morning of surgery is still one of the commonest reasons for a cancelled list, even though the link between pre-operative hypertension and perioperative harm is weak below very high values. The 2016 Association of Anaesthetists and British Hypertension Society guideline set a clinic cut-off of 180/110 mmHg; this is the planned update, now with the British and Irish Hypertension Society (McCormack and colleagues, Anaesthesia, online 14 January 2026).

**What they did.** An expert working party ran a targeted literature review and a modified Delphi process. Scope: adults having planned surgery other than cardiothoracic, obstetric or endocrine procedures, from the decision to operate to 30 days after surgery.

**What it says.**
- Secondary care should accept a referral that documents a clinic BP below 160/100 mmHg, or an ambulatory or home BP below 155/95 mmHg, within 12 months.
- A patient arriving at pre-operative assessment without a documented primary-care reading may proceed if the clinic BP is below 180/120 mmHg, or an out-of-office reading is below 175/115 mmHg.
- Out-of-office measurement is given equal standing with clinic readings, and the document covers measurement, referral back to primary care and perioperative management.
- A short companion paper from the same group (Frank and colleagues, Anaesthesia, online 19 March 2026) addresses which antihypertensives to continue or hold.

**Caveats.** Consensus-based and UK-focused; the thresholds are about proceeding safely, not about intraoperative targets, which still rest on the individual patient's baseline. Cardiac surgery is explicitly out of scope.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** Fewer same-day cancellations for isolated readings in the 160-180 systolic range, a defined role for home monitoring, and a clear message that long-term control belongs to primary care rather than to the pre-op clinic.
editorTakeHome: Referral accepted with clinic BP under 160/100, or ambulatory/home under 155/95, documented within 12 months
No primary-care record: proceed if clinic BP is under 180/120 or home/ambulatory under 175/115
Scope is adults having planned non-cardiothoracic, non-obstetric, non-endocrine surgery, decision to operate to 30 days after
authorLimitations: No full systematic review or quantitative/qualitative synthesis of the identified evidence was performed.
Many recommendations were supported by weak or modest evidence, limiting the authors' ability to formally grade them.
Given the lack of high-quality evidence, especially for the peri-operative period, many recommendations were designed with pragmatism in mind.

posts.headline: AHA standardizes right heart cath protocols: LVAD ramp targets CVP under 12, PAWP under 18, CI over 2.2
posts.summary: An AHA scientific statement (Belkin, chair) sets common protocols for baseline, provocative and serial invasive hemodynamics in heart failure and pulmonary hypertension, including vasoreactivity testing before transplant, fluid and exercise challenges, LVAD ramp studies and when a PA catheter earns its place.
takeHome: Diagnosis and management of cardiogenic shock, HFpEF, pulmonary hypertension and LVAD support require resting and provocative invasive testing, often serially
Statement provides evidence-based rationale and practical protocols to standardize resting and provocative right heart catheterization, including vasodilator, volume and exercise challenges
Ramp, reverse-ramp and exercise studies in LVAD patients are detailed; authors call for cross-disciplinary collaboration, standardization and investment in emerging technologies
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Right heart catheterization numbers drive transplant listing, LVAD settings and the liver transplant go or no-go in portopulmonary hypertension, yet protocols vary from lab to lab. This AHA statement, in Circulation: Heart Failure (19:e000088) in January 2026 with Belkin as chair and Fudim as vice chair, sets common ground for static, provocative and serial measurements in heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, LVAD patients and cardiogenic shock.

**What it says.**
- Pre-transplant: pulmonary hypertension predicts 30-day mortality after heart transplant. Test reversibility with sodium nitroprusside or a milrinone bolus; inhaled nitric oxide can be used when wedge pressure is not elevated.
- Occult post-capillary PH: when resting numbers do not explain dyspnea, a fluid bolus or passive leg raise can unmask it. Invasive exercise testing identifies the cause of exertional symptoms; exercise-induced PH predicts outcome but is not yet a treatment target.
- Acute vasoreactivity testing in suspected idiopathic, heritable or drug-induced PAH: inhaled prostacyclin analogs or NO preferred; a positive response is a fall in mean PA pressure of 10 mm Hg or more to below 40 mm Hg without a drop in cardiac output.
- Magnetically levitated LVADs: invasive ramp and reverse-ramp studies are preferred over echo alone, targeting CVP under 12 mm Hg, PAWP under 18 mm Hg and cardiac index above 2.2 L/min/m2, which track with fewer admissions and hemocompatibility events.
- Continuous PA catheter monitoring is useful in advanced PH or RV dysfunction during high-risk procedures, LVAD implantation, pulmonary endarterectomy and liver transplantation with portopulmonary hypertension; routine early PAC use in cardiogenic shock still needs data.

**For the anesthesiologist.** This is the reference for the pre-transplant vasodilator study, the LVAD ramp you are asked to supervise, and the argument for a PA catheter in the POPH liver transplant.
editorTakeHome: Pre-transplant PH reversibility: test with nitroprusside or a milrinone bolus, inhaled NO if PAWP is not elevated; PH predicts 30-day post-transplant death
Maglev LVAD optimization: invasive ramp and reverse-ramp studies over echo alone, aiming for CVP under 12, PAWP under 18, CI over 2.2
Continuous PAC monitoring endorsed for advanced PH or RV dysfunction in high-risk procedures, LVAD implant, pulmonary endarterectomy and POPH liver transplant

posts.headline: EACTAIC issues its first consensus on monitoring in thoracic anaesthesia, from basic monitors to NMB and brain
posts.summary: A 45-author EACTAIC task force has published consensus recommendations on what to monitor during thoracic anaesthesia, covering respiratory, circulatory, neuromuscular and neurological monitoring in routine and specialised settings. It is the first of a series of thoracic consensus documents.
takeHome: First of a series from the EACTAIC Thoracic Subcommittee Monitoring Task Force: structured expert opinion on monitoring as the core task in thoracic anaesthesia.
Covers basic vs advanced monitoring, respiratory and circulatory monitoring, neuromuscular blockade, depth of anaesthesia and neurologic function, and research priorities.
All recommendations reached agreed (>60%), strong (>80%) or full (>95%) consensus among senior clinicians from Europe, the US, Africa and the Middle East.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Thoracic anaesthesia has lacked a society document on which monitors belong in the room, when advanced haemodynamic or neuromonitoring is worth it, and how to interpret it during one-lung ventilation. EACTAIC's Thoracic Subcommittee has now published the first of a planned series of consensus documents, written by its General Management: Monitoring Task Force.

**What they did.** Senior thoracic anaesthesiologists from Europe, the United States, Africa and the Middle East (45 named authors) reviewed the evidence and voted on statements. Agreement is reported in three tiers: agreed (more than 60%), strong (more than 80%) and, for some statements, full consensus (more than 95%).

**What it covers.**
- Standard basic and advanced monitoring for thoracic patients
- Respiratory and circulatory monitoring in routine and specialised settings
- Monitoring of neuromuscular blockade, depth of anaesthesia and neurological function
- Research priorities, and how monitoring links to good clinical practice and enhanced recovery after lung surgery

**Caveats.** The authors are candid that high-level evidence is limited and that controversies remain; the document consolidates diverse practice rather than settling it. Nothing here is a randomised result, and some statements reached only the lowest consensus tier.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** This is the reference to cite when standardising a thoracic monitoring bundle, deciding on arterial and central access, or arguing for quantitative neuromuscular and depth-of-anaesthesia monitoring in a lung-resection pathway. Read it alongside the companion EACTAIC airway document published in the same month. Print version: J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth 2026;40(3):985-993.
authorLimitations: High-level evidence base is generally limited and significant controversies remain; the document represents the structured opinions of delegated experts.
editorTakeHome: First European consensus on monitoring for thoracic cases; use it to audit your lung-resection and OLV monitoring bundle.
Recommendations are graded by agreement level: agreed (>60%), strong (>80%) and full (>95%) consensus.
Authors stress the evidence base is thin, so treat this as a shared baseline rather than a rulebook.

posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Lung isolation is the defining skill of thoracic anaesthesia, yet choices between double-lumen tubes and bronchial blockers, and plans for the patient with both a difficult airway and a need for one-lung ventilation, have mostly rested on local habit. This EACTAIC document gives the subspecialty a shared reference.

**What they did.** The Airway Management Task Force of the EACTAIC Thoracic Subcommittee (around 40 authors, the TOSSCA Consensus Group) reviewed the evidence and had senior clinicians from Europe, the United States, Africa and the Middle East evaluate the statements. Consensus is reported as agreed (more than 60%), strong (more than 80%) and, in places, full (more than 95%).

**What it covers.** Six clinical questions:
- The goals of lung isolation and the means of achieving separation
- Best practice for double-lumen tubes
- The role of bronchial blockers
- Management of the difficult airway in thoracic surgery
- Special cases
- Research priorities

It compares the benefits and drawbacks of each device in routine and difficult scenarios and ties the recommendations to good clinical practice and enhanced recovery.

**Caveats.** As with the monitoring document, the authors state that high-level evidence is generally limited and that significant controversies remain. The abstract does not give a count of recommendations, and some statements sit at the lowest agreement tier.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** Use it to standardise device selection and sizing, to write the difficult-airway-plus-OLV algorithm every thoracic unit should have on the wall, and as the citation when a surgeon asks why a blocker was chosen. posts.headline: DESIGNATION: driving pressure-guided PEEP plus recruitment did not cut pulmonary complications after abdominal surgery
posts.summary: Across 29 European sites, 1,435 adults at increased pulmonary risk having open abdominal surgery were randomised to individualised PEEP titrated to the lowest driving pressure plus recruitment manoeuvres, or fixed PEEP 5 without recruitment; the composite of pulmonary complications within 5 days was 19.8% vs 17.4%.
takeHome: Pulmonary complications within 5 days: 19.8% high PEEP vs 17.4% low PEEP (absolute difference 2.5%, 95% CI -1.5% to 6.4%; P = .23)
High PEEP group had more hypotension (54.0% vs 45.0%) and vasoactive use (32.0% vs 18.8%); low PEEP more desaturation (2.8% vs 0.8%)
Authors conclude driving pressure-guided high PEEP with recruitment maneuvers did not reduce postoperative pulmonary complications versus standard low PEEP
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** After PROVHILO and iPROVE, the individualised ventilation camp argued that PEEP should be titrated to each patient's mechanics using driving pressure rather than set high or low for everyone. DESIGNATION, from the PROVE Network, is the definitive test of that idea in open abdominal surgery, and it reported three weeks after PROTHOR delivered the same verdict for one-lung ventilation.

**What they did.** Investigator-initiated trial at 29 sites in five European countries, April 2019 to December 2024. Adults with ARISCAT 26 or higher and BMI up to 40 having open abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia were randomised to volume-controlled ventilation at 8 mL/kg predicted body weight with either a recruitment manoeuvre followed by decremental PEEP titration to the lowest driving pressure (default 12 cmH2O), repeated at set points including before extubation, or fixed PEEP 5 cmH2O with no recruitment. Outcome assessors were blinded; 1,435 patients were analysed.

**What they found.**
- Composite of pulmonary complications within 5 days: 19.8% vs 17.4%, absolute difference 2.5% (95% CI -1.5 to 6.4; P = 0.23).
- Intraoperative hypotension 54.0% vs 45.0%; vasoactive drug use 32.0% vs 18.8%.
- Desaturation 0.8% vs 2.8%; unplanned ICU admission 1.3% vs 2.5% (not significant); hospital mortality 3.6% vs 3.3%.
- Patients already planned for ICU or HDU had more complications with high PEEP (33.9% vs 23.6%, interaction P = 0.007), a hypothesis-generating signal.

**Caveats.** Event rates were below the planning assumptions, so the interval does not exclude a small benefit or harm; clinicians could not be blinded; the comparator was already lung-protective.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** Better mechanics and oxygenation on the monitor did not translate into fewer complications and cost more pressors. Low tidal volume with PEEP 5 remains the default; individualised PEEP is for rescue of the hypoxaemic patient, not routine.
posts.firstAuthor: Writing and Steering Committees for the DESIGNATION Investigators
editorTakeHome: Postoperative pulmonary complications 19.8% vs 17.4% (difference 2.5%, 95% CI -1.5 to 6.4); hospital mortality 3.6% vs 3.3%
High PEEP caused more hypotension (54% vs 45%) and vasopressor use (32% vs 19%), with less desaturation (0.8% vs 2.8%)
With PROTHOR in thoracic surgery, that is two large trials: tidal volume 8 mL/kg, PEEP 5, no routine recruitment

posts.headline: ERS/ESTS replace the 2009 lung resection fitness algorithm: DLCO for everyone, ppoFEV1 or ppoDLCO under 40% is high risk
posts.summary: The first full rewrite of the ERS/ESTS fitness guideline, co-published in ERJ and EJCTS and endorsed by ESAIC, makes DLCO a strong recommendation for every surgical candidate, calls for routine predicted postoperative values, and sets field-test and CPET thresholds.
takeHome: ERS/ESTS panel with patient representatives addressed four PICO and seven narrative questions on fitness for curative-intent lung cancer treatment
Evidence graded with GRADE after QUIPS risk-of-bias assessment; recommendations framed with the Evidence to Decisions framework
Recommendations cover pulmonary function testing, split lung function, exercise testing, cardiac testing, prehabilitation, sublobar resection, risk scores and comorbidities
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The 2009 ERS/ESTS algorithm has decided who is offered a lung resection for 16 years. This replacement, chaired by Brunelli, Hardavella and Huber, was co-published in the European Respiratory Journal (66:2500156) and the European Journal of Cardio-Thoracic Surgery in November 2025 and endorsed by ESAIC, ESTRO and IASLC. Its scope now covers radiotherapy and systemic treatment as well as surgery, plus nutrition, frailty, prehabilitation and sublobar resection.

**What they did.** A multidisciplinary panel with patient representatives answered four PICO and seven narrative questions with GRADE and an evidence-to-decision framework.

**What changed.**
- DLCO for every surgical candidate is now a strong recommendation, and ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO should be calculated routinely rather than only when spirometry is impaired. Bands: DLCO 60-79% mild, 40-59% moderate, under 40% high; ppoFEV1 or ppoDLCO under 40% high, 40-59% moderate.
- Repeat FEV1 and DLCO after neoadjuvant therapy; post-induction DLCO or ppo values under 80% signal higher risk.
- One low-technology test screens exercise capacity: a 6-minute or shuttle walk above 400 m or a stair climb above 10 m suggests low risk, and poor performers are referred for CPET.
- CPET: VO2peak below 12 mL/kg/min or a VE/VCO2 slope above 40 suggests high surgical risk, with no single parameter mandated.
- Do not select on a risk score alone (EuroLung 2 is for benchmarking). Assess nutrition when BMI is under 18.5, weight loss is 10% or more, or age is over 70; screen frailty after 60. Prehabilitation can reduce pulmonary complications in high-risk patients (moderate certainty). Offer smoking cessation. Age alone should not decide treatment.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Expect ppo values and a field test in every thoracic clinic note, and expect to anesthetize patients the 2009 rules would have declined, now with prehabilitation and sublobar options on the table.
editorTakeHome: DLCO in every surgical candidate; ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO calculated routinely, with under 40% high risk and 40-59% moderate
One field test screens: walk over 400 m or stair climb over 10 m suggests low risk; poor performers go to CPET
CPET: VO2peak under 12 mL/kg/min or VE/VCO2 slope over 40 flags high risk; repeat FEV1 and DLCO after neoadjuvant therapy

posts.headline: Delirium is coded after 1 in 20 US CABGs and rising; it nearly doubles in-hospital death and adds 4 days and $8,565
posts.summary: In 911,910 isolated CABG admissions from the National Inpatient Sample (2016-2021), coded postoperative delirium occurred in 4.9% and rose each year. Delirium carried an adjusted 1.85-fold higher in-hospital mortality, four extra days in hospital and $8,565 in added cost.
takeHome: Among 911,910 US CABG hospitalisations (National Inpatient Sample 2016-2021), ICD-10-coded postoperative delirium occurred in 4.91%, rising each year (OR 1.04 per year).
Strongest adjusted associations: pre-existing dementia (aOR 4.28), alcohol abuse (aOR 3.38) and psychotic disorders (aOR 2.40).
Delirium was independently associated with higher mortality (aOR 1.85), major complications, a four-day longer stay and $8,565 higher costs.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Delirium after cardiac surgery is common, but national-scale numbers on trend, risk and cost have been scarce. This NIS analysis gives anaesthesiologists citable figures for prevention programmes and for the preoperative conversation with high-risk patients.

**What they did.** Retrospective analysis of the US National Inpatient Sample, 2016-2021, using discharge weights. Adults with isolated CABG were identified, and postoperative delirium was defined by validated ICD-10 codes. Multivariable models adjusted for patient and hospital factors.

**What they found.**
- 911,910 weighted CABG hospitalisations; delirium coded in 4.91%
- Incidence rose over the period (OR 1.04 per year, p < 0.001)
- Strongest independent predictors: pre-existing dementia (aOR 4.28), alcohol abuse (aOR 3.38), psychotic disorders (aOR 2.40)
- Delirium was independently associated with in-hospital death (aOR 1.85), more major complications, a 4-day longer stay and $8,565 higher cost (all p < 0.001)

**Caveats.** Administrative coding under-detects delirium: prospective screening studies after cardiac surgery report far higher rates, so the 4.9% is a floor, and the rising trend may partly reflect better documentation. Associations with mortality are adjusted but not causal, and the dataset lacks STS-style physiological risk variables, anaesthetic technique and sedation data.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** The risk-factor profile is actionable at the preoperative visit: cognitive screening, alcohol history and psychiatric medication review identify who needs the full delirium bundle (avoid benzodiazepines, multimodal analgesia, early mobilisation, sleep protection). The cost figure makes the business case. Print version: J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth 2026;40(2):561-570.
editorTakeHome: Dementia (aOR 4.28), alcohol misuse (3.38) and psychotic disorders (2.40) flag the highest-risk CABG patients before induction.
Coded delirium is rising about 4% a year; expect the true screened incidence to be several times higher.
Cost and length-of-stay numbers are useful ammunition for funding a delirium prevention bundle.

posts.headline: ELSO issues a dedicated narrative guideline on ECMO for pregnant and peripartum patients
posts.summary: An international ELSO writing group led by Erika O'Neil, with Emily Naoum, Marc Anders, Kollengode Ramanathan and Matteo Di Nardo, publishes ELSO's guidance on extracorporeal support of pregnant and recently delivered patients in the November 2025 ASAIO Journal.
takeHome: One ELSO reference now exists for peripartum ECMO; read it before the next amniotic fluid embolism or peripartum cardiomyopathy arrives
A narrative guideline: structured expert guidance on practices ELSO considers useful and safe, not a GRADE document or standard of care
Same issue carries ELSO's accidental hypothermia guideline; both were released by ELSO in October 2025
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Peripartum collapse is where obstetric and cardiac anesthesia meet: amniotic fluid embolism, peripartum cardiomyopathy, massive hemorrhage with arrest, and severe ARDS in a patient whose physiology, airway, anticoagulation and fetus all complicate the usual ECMO rules. Until now ELSO had no guideline specific to pregnancy. This narrative guideline fills that gap, published in ASAIO Journal 71(11):875-887 (November 2025, online 24 September 2025) by an international writing group led by Erika O'Neil, with Ahmed Labib Shehatta, Cara Agerstrand, Caroline Sampson, Farah Siddiqui, Priya Nair, Alexandra Schou, Javier Kattan, Emily Naoum, Marc Anders, Kollengode Ramanathan and Matteo Di Nardo.

**What it is.** ELSO's narrative guidelines are structured expert documents rather than GRADE-graded recommendations. ELSO describes them as educational, built on practices it believes are useful and safe, based on the data available when written, and due for revision as evidence accrues; they explicitly do not guarantee an outcome or define a standard of care.

**What to do with it.** Use it to build the pathway before the case rather than during it: who cannulates and where, which configuration, how anticoagulation and bleeding risk are weighed against the uterus and the surgical field, and how delivery is planned around the circuit. A short list of named roles, the multidisciplinary call tree, and a stocked cannulation cart on the labor floor are the kind of practical steps a document like this is meant to prompt.

**Caveat.** The full text sits behind the ASAIO Journal paywall; this post rests on the citation, the author list and the guideline's stated scope, not on a line-by-line read. Pull the PDF through your library before writing local protocol from it.

posts.headline: ELSO: ECLS for hypothermic arrest below 30 C when HOPE survival is 10% or more; rewarm at up to 5 C per hour
posts.summary: ELSO's 2025 narrative guideline on accidental hypothermia (Cools and Swol, first authors) sets who goes on the pump, favors femoro-femoral VA-ECMO with a distal perfusion cannula, and gives rewarming and weaning targets.
takeHome: Hypothermic arrest: ECLS if core temperature is under 30 C and HOPE survival probability is 10% or more; measure core temperature esophageally
Unwitnessed arrest, asystole, long no-flow, age over 70 and low EtCO2 are not contraindications; consider stopping without ROSC at 32-35 C
Rewarm up to 5 C/h; oxygenator gradient 4 C or less; heater at most 10 C above venous inflow, max 42 C
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Hypothermic cardiac arrest is the one arrest where hours of CPR can end with an intact brain, and the decision to cannulate usually falls to whoever is on call for ECMO. ELSO's narrative guideline, in ASAIO Journal 71:865-874 (November 2025 issue), puts the triage and the circuit settings in one place.

**Who goes on.** Hypothermic arrest with core temperature below 30 C and an estimated HOPE survival probability of 10% or more is an indication; below 30 C there is no absolute contraindication. Core temperature 30-32 C or HOPE below 10% is exceptional-case territory. Measure core temperature with an esophageal probe. Unwitnessed arrest, asystole, long no-flow or low-flow times, age 70 or over and low EtCO2 do not exclude a patient; potassium feeds the HOPE score rather than acting as a stand-alone cut-off.

**How to run it.** Femoro-femoral VA-ECMO with a distal perfusion cannula is preferred: fewer resources, less heparin, possibly better outcomes; cardiopulmonary bypass is reasonable if ECMO is unavailable. Switch to VAV if differential oxygenation appears. Rewarm at up to 5 C per hour until 30 C or ROSC, keeping the oxygenator venous-to-arterial gradient at 4 C or less and the heater no more than 10 C above venous inflow, maximum 42 C. Consider stopping if there is no ROSC at 32-35 C. Wean once core temperature exceeds 35 C with improved LV function on echo, stepping flow to 50% then 25%; weaning succeeds in 30-70%.

**The numbers.** Survival after hypothermic arrest ranges from 37% to 85%, with good neurologic outcome in 80-90% of survivors. In ICE-CRASH, ECMO was associated with better 28-day survival (OR 0.17) and neurologic outcome (OR 0.22). Notify the ECLS center from the scene; long transport with ongoing CPR is no reason to withhold resuscitation.

posts.headline: EACVI/ACVC/EACTAIC set five tiers of cardiac ultrasound for emergency and ICU care, with focused TEE for ECMO and CPR
posts.summary: A joint consensus from the ESC imaging and acute care associations and the cardiothoracic anaesthesia society sorts cardiac ultrasound into FoCUS, emergency echo, targeted echo, critical care echo and focused TEE, and tabulates the cut-offs for shock and RV assessment.
takeHome: Pathophysiology-based framework for cardiac ultrasound in cardiogenic shock, acute MI and mechanical complications, acute heart failure, valve disease, tamponade, pulmonary embolism and cardiac arrest
Describes key modalities, measurement techniques and diagnostic criteria; stresses integrating cardiac ultrasound with multimodal and organ-specific ultrasound
Proposes training pathways, competency levels and governance to support quality and limit medicolegal exposure; anticipates AI and big-data applications
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The last EACVI emergency echo document predates modern shock teams and ECMO programs. This update, with the Acute CardioVascular Care Association and EACTAIC as co-authors, extends it into cardiac critical care. It went online 21 August 2025 and appears in the November 2025 issue of European Heart Journal - Cardiovascular Imaging (26:1699-1724; Soliman Aboumarie and Tavazzi, joint first authors), with a correction in March 2026.

**Who scans what.** Five levels: FoCUS by operators trained in focused ultrasound who are often the decision-maker; emergency echo by fully trained echocardiographers producing a complete dataset; targeted echo answering a specific question; critical care echo requiring advanced training; and focused TEE requiring comprehensive TEE training. Focused TEE earns its place when transthoracic windows fail, for dissection and endocarditis, for guiding ECMO and MCS cannulation and weaning, and during CPR. LVOT VTI is taken from transgastric views at 0 or 120 degrees.

**Scenarios.** Cardiac arrest: look for tamponade, PE and hypovolemia, but scanning that interferes with compressions is not appropriate. Shock: separate cardiac from non-cardiac causes, assess effusion, ventricular function, valves and volume, with cardiogenic shock staged by SCAI-type categories including post-cardiotomy.

**The numbers.** Normal LVOT VTI 18-22 cm, averaged over about 10 beats in AF. RV: TAPSE 16 mm or less, S' under 9.5 cm/s, FAC under 35%, RVEF under 45%, free-wall strain worse than -23%, RV/LV ratio over 0.6, TR velocity over 2.8 m/s, IVC over 2.1 cm with under 50% collapse. Ejection fraction is not validated in critical care, and every parameter moves with load, heart rate and operator.

**For the perioperative TEE reader.** This is the document to cite when defining who may do a focused TEE on a VA-ECMO patient at 2 am, and what training that requires.
editorTakeHome: Five tiers by training: FoCUS, emergency echo, targeted echo, critical care echo (advanced) and focused TEE (comprehensive TEE training)
Focused TEE for ECMO and MCS cannulation, troubleshooting and weaning, for CPR, and when windows fail; LVOT VTI from transgastric views
Scan during CPR only for reversible causes without interrupting compressions; EF is not validated in critical care and every index is load-dependent

posts.headline: ERC/ESICM 2025: keep post-arrest temperature at or below 37.5 C for 72 h; no ST elevation means CT first, cath lab later
posts.summary: The joint European post-resuscitation care guideline (Nolan and colleagues, Intensive Care Medicine and Resuscitation, 22 October 2025) replaces targeted hypothermia with fever prevention, puts dual-phase head-to-pelvis CT ahead of coronary angiography when there is no ST elevation, sets MAP above 60-65 mmHg, and extends multimodal prognostication to every patient with a motor score of 5 or less.
takeHome: Targets: SpO2 94-98%, PaCO2 35-45 mmHg, MAP over 60-65, temperature 37.5 C or lower for 72 h; no 32-34 C
No ST elevation after OHCA: delay catheterisation unless acute occlusion is likely; dual-phase head-to-pelvis CT with CTPA
Prognosticate at 72 h or later with two or more signs: pupils and corneals, SSEP, malignant EEG, NSE over 60, myoclonus, imaging
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** This document defines how a comatose post-arrest patient is run in European ICUs, including the ECPR patient you cannulated. Written by the ERC and ESICM, it appeared simultaneously in Intensive Care Medicine and Resuscitation on 22 October 2025, alongside the AHA 2025 guidelines.

**What is new since 2021.**
- Temperature control replaces targeted temperature management: actively prevent fever at or below 37.5 C for 36 to 72 hours (the summary table says at least 72), do not rewarm mild spontaneous hypothermia, and do not target 32-34 C.
- Cause: emergent cath lab for persistent ST elevation; otherwise delay catheterisation unless acute occlusion is likely, and obtain dual-phase head-to-pelvis CT including pulmonary angiography.
- Explicit targets: SpO2 94-98% (PaO2 75-100 mmHg), PaCO2 35-45 mmHg with a consistent temperature-correction approach when cold, tidal volume 6-8 mL/kg, MAP above 60-65 mmHg with an arterial line and early echo; no routine steroids or prophylactic antibiotics.
- Mechanical circulatory support may be considered for persistent cardiogenic shock despite drugs, preferentially with GCS 8 or more on arrival, STEMI and a short arrest.
- Prognostication applies to all patients with a motor score below 6 at 72 hours or later, after confounders are excluded; poor outcome is likely with two or more of absent pupillary and corneal reflexes, bilaterally absent N20, highly malignant EEG, NSE above 60 micrograms/L at 48-72 h, status myoclonus, or diffuse anoxic injury on CT or MRI.

**Caveats.** Most recommendations rest on low-certainty evidence, the temperature duration is stated inconsistently, and the AHA document published the same day allows 32-37.5 C.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** For the patient who arrested in your OR or on your ECMO: arterial line, echo, normoxia and normocapnia, fever prevention rather than cooling, and no prognostic statements to the family before 72 hours.

posts.headline: WSES-AAST thoracic trauma guidelines: rib fixation within 48-72 h when indicated, drain haemothorax of 500 mL or more
posts.summary: The World Society of Emergency Surgery and AAST issued graded recommendations for the whole chest-trauma pathway, from needle or finger decompression and chest-tube sizing to rib fixation timing, operative thresholds for bleeding, tracheobronchial and diaphragm injury, ventilation and VV-ECMO (Coccolini and colleagues, World Journal of Emergency Surgery, 15 October 2025).
takeHome: Drain stable hemothorax of 500 mL or more; operate for instability from thoracic bleeding, over 1,500 mL/24 h, or 200 mL/h for 3 hours
Rib fixation within 48-72 hours for stable flail chest, 3 or more severely displaced fractures of ribs 3-10, or failed weaning; instability contraindicates it
Tracheobronchial injury: secure the airway first, with bronchoscopy guidance if possible; VV-ECMO is viable when conventional ventilation fails (reported survival 68.4%)
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Chest injury runs through the emergency department, the OR and the ICU. This WSES-AAST document grades the whole pathway and belongs next to the ACS chest wall injury guideline and the SOFRIB trial.

**What they did.** A literature search from 2000 to February 2024 excluded opinion pieces and small series. Statements carry a level of evidence (high to very low) and a grade of recommendation (strong, moderate or weak), agreed by WSES and AAST experts through a three-round modified Delphi.

**Key recommendations.**
- Tension pneumothorax: immediate needle (second space midclavicular or fifth midaxillary) or finger decompression (moderate, strong). A chest tube at the fourth to sixth space is the treatment of choice (moderate, strong); small-bore suffices for air, 28-40 Fr for blood, nothing gained above 32 Fr.
- Stable patients: observe a pneumothorax up to 2 cm or haemothorax under 300 mL for 24 hours; drain 500 mL or more.
- Operate for haemodynamic instability or bleeding over 1,500 mL initially or over 200 mL/h for three hours (low, strong).
- Rib fixation: consider for stable flail chest and for three or more severely displaced fractures or failure to wean (moderate, moderate); perform within 48-72 hours (high, strong); haemodynamic instability is a contraindication (moderate, strong).
- Epidural and multimodal analgesia are conditionally recommended; paravertebral and fascial plane blocks are not graded.
- Tracheobronchial injury: airway first, bronchoscopy-guided intubation, surgery for large ruptures or persistent leak (moderate, strong).
- VV-ECMO is a viable option when conventional ventilation fails.

**Caveats.** Surgeon-led; REBOA, resuscitative thoracotomy and aortic injury targets get only passing mention, and the analgesia section is thin.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** The fixation timing rule and the thresholds for taking a bleeding chest to theatre shape your day; for regional analgesia, keep the ACS guidance as the reference.
editorTakeHome: Operate for instability, bleeding over 1,500 mL initially or 200 mL/h for 3 h; drain haemothorax of 500 mL or more
Consider fixation for stable flail chest, 3 or more displaced fractures or failed weaning, ideally at 48-72 h; instability contraindicates it
Tracheobronchial injury: secure the airway first with bronchoscopy-guided intubation; VV-ECMO is an option when ventilation fails
authorLimitations: Few data exist on intrapleural thrombolytics and none define a safe residual hemothorax volume; non-invasive ventilation's effect in blunt chest injury is uncertain
Epidural and multimodal analgesia are only conditionally recommended, despite some limitations; little evidence addresses rib fixation safety in elderly patients

posts.headline: Children with heart disease having noncardiac surgery: mid-volume hospitals, not the smallest, had the highest mortality
posts.summary: Across 662,680 noncardiac surgical admissions in the Pediatric Health Information System (2016-2023), in-hospital mortality was highest at mid-volume children's hospitals, including 6.3% in children with complex congenital heart disease, rather than following a simple low-volume-is-worse pattern.
takeHome: PHIS 2016-2023: 662,680 patients; 23,712 simple, 16,243 complex and 5,329 single-ventricle CHD; hospitals grouped into CHD-volume quintiles
Mortality peaked at mid-volume quintile 3: 0.83% overall, 0.56% non-CHD, 6.28% complex CHD; similar across quintiles for simple and single-ventricle lesions
Adjusted odds of in-hospital death higher at quintile 3 (OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.01-1.3); authors say reasons and regionalization implications need study
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Children with congenital heart disease (CHD) increasingly present for noncardiac surgery outside dedicated cardiac centres, and it has been assumed that higher-volume hospitals do better. This national paediatric database study challenges that assumption and will shape the regionalisation debate.

**What they did.** Retrospective analysis of the Pediatric Health Information System, 2016-2023, covering 662,680 children undergoing noncardiac surgery: 617,396 without CHD, 23,712 with simple heart disease, 16,243 with complex CHD and 5,329 with single-ventricle physiology. Hospitals were split into quintiles by the number of CHD patients they took to noncardiac procedures (quintile 1 under 500; quintile 3 between 900 and 1,100; quintile 5 over 1,500).

**What they found.**
- In-hospital mortality was highest in quintile 3 for the whole cohort (0.83%), for children without CHD (0.56%) and for complex CHD (6.28%)
- Mortality did not differ by volume for simple lesions or single-ventricle disease
- In multivariable analysis, quintile 3 remained associated with higher mortality (adjusted OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.01-1.30)
- Length of stay varied without a consistent pattern

**Caveats.** PHIS captures only tertiary children's hospitals, so the lowest-volume community settings are absent. Volume was defined by CHD noncardiac procedures, not by cardiac-anaesthesia staffing or ICU capability, and administrative data cannot explain why mid-volume centres fared worse; the authors call for further study before drawing regionalisation conclusions.

**For the anaesthesiologist.** The 6% mortality in complex CHD is the number to remember when triaging who needs a cardiac anaesthesiologist and a cardiac ICU bed for a seemingly minor procedure. Volume alone is not a proxy for safety. Print version: J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth 2026;40(1):143-150.
editorTakeHome: Volume-outcome logic from cardiac surgery does not transfer cleanly to noncardiac surgery in CHD children.
Complex CHD carried 6.3% in-hospital mortality at mid-volume centres; single-ventricle outcomes were similar across volume groups.
Regionalisation arguments need more than volume; team structure and case selection likely matter more.

posts.headline: UK ECMO emergency guideline: arrest on ECMO means MAP under 30, fix the circuit before drugs, CPR is safe on support
posts.summary: All UK ECMO centres and eight national societies, including the Resuscitation Council UK and ACTACC, used a five-round Delphi to produce a single adult ECMO emergency algorithm: confirm arrest by a working arterial line reading under 30 mmHg, split into patient and ECMO teams, restore flow first, and compress the chest when circulation is inadequate.
takeHome: Cardiac arrest on ECMO: unresponsive and/or not breathing normally plus confirmed MAP below 30 mmHg; sudden ETCO2 fall and absent flow are supportive
Priority in a device-dependent patient is restoring flow: expose circuit, check kinks and cannulae; if no flow, clamp the return line and follow SOPs
No evidence CPR harms ECMO patients with inadequate circulation; adequate circulation is MAP above 55 mmHg, flow above 2 L/min, SpO2 above 88%
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Standard ALS assumes a native circulation. On ECMO, pulselessness is normal, ETCO2 is unreliable, and perfusion usually returns by fixing a kinked line, not by giving adrenaline.

**What they did.** Akhtar and colleagues (Intensive Care Medicine, online 6 October 2025) convened all UK ECMO centres and eight societies, including ACTACC, the Intensive Care Society, SCTS and the Resuscitation Council UK. With only 15 usable studies, recommendations are graded with the ESC class and level system, mostly IIa C, after five Delphi rounds.

**The algorithm.**
- Recognition: unresponsive or not breathing normally, with a confirmed MAP below 30 mmHg on a levelled, working transducer; an ETCO2 drop and lost flow support it.
- One leader, two teams. The ECMO team exposes the patient, inspects circuit and cannulae and straightens kinks; the patient team runs standard ALS. Fixing the device comes first (Class I).
- Low flow with suction: reduce RPM until chatter stops, then increase to the best tolerated flow; consider a 2.5 mL/kg bolus, the bleeding protocol and echo.
- No flow: clamp the return line, then follow the SOP for air embolus, motor failure (new console or hand-crank), rupture or decannulation.
- Compressions are safe on ECMO and should be given when circulation is inadequate; use reduced or infused adrenaline when troubleshooting will restore flow quickly; consider re-sternotomy within 10 days of cardiac surgery.
- Reassess: adequate is MAP above 55 mmHg, flow above 2 L/min and SpO2 above 88%; intermediate values prompt a circuit-change decision, echo, or escalation (more Impella support, VV to VVA).

**Caveats.** Nearly all recommendations are expert consensus (level C) and UK-specific; mechanical compression devices and defibrillation are not addressed.

**For us.** Print the algorithm, simulate it, and make the transducer rule and clamp-first sequence identical on every ECMO bed.
editorTakeHome: Arrest on ECMO: unresponsive plus confirmed MAP under 30 mmHg; falling ETCO2 and lost flow support the call
Priority is restoring flow: expose, check kinks and cannulae, clamp the return line if flow does not return, follow the fault SOP
Adequate circulation is MAP over 55, flow over 2 L/min, SpO2 over 88%; consider re-sternotomy within 10 days of surgery
authorLimitations: The MAP 30 mmHg arrest threshold and the 55 mmHg, 2 L/min and 88% circulation targets are consensus judgements, not evidence-derived
Only 15 studies were included from 1,257 screened; almost all recommendations are level C (observational data and expert consensus)
CPR safety on ECMO rests on absence of evidence of harm; mechanical compression devices have no safety evidence with MCS
ETCO2 is unreliable on ECMO and can only support other signs; the search was limited to English-language adult studies

posts.headline: US-CRS: a lab-and-device urgency score ranks heart transplant candidates better than the six-status system
posts.summary: SRTR registry study of about 38,000 adult US heart transplant candidates (2019-2025) built and tested a continuous 6-week waitlist mortality score, then replayed 45,530 donor match runs against the current six-status system.
takeHome: Score built from 5 laboratory values and 4 therapies (durable LVAD, IABP, microaxial pump, advanced MCS) in 21,859 training candidates.
Time-dependent AUC for 6-week mortality 0.807 with US-CRS vs 0.693 for current statuses in the test set; calibration acceptable, including exception statuses.
Simulated reallocation of 45,530 hearts moved 67% of recipients down; first-ranked candidates' 6-week mortality rose from 11.2% to 15.7%, prioritising sicker patients.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** About one in five US heart transplant candidates dies or is delisted before an organ arrives, and the therapy-based six-status system rewards escalation: a balloon pump or a temporary pump moves a patient up whether or not their physiology demands it. OPTN has been working toward continuous distribution, and this is the medical-urgency engine proposed for it.

**What they did.** Lyden and colleagues used SRTR data on adult candidates listed from January 2019 to August 2025, split by time into training (21,859), validation (7,897) and test (8,256) sets. A marginal structural model estimated 6-week mortality without transplant. The final US Candidate Risk Score keeps 5 laboratory values and 4 device categories: durable LVAD, IABP, microaxial flow pump and advanced mechanical circulatory support. They then simulated 45,530 match runs with the score in place of statuses.

**What they found.**
- Mean time-dependent AUC for death within 6 weeks was 0.807 with US-CRS versus 0.693 with the status system; calibration was acceptable, including for exception-status candidates.
- Reordering by US-CRS moved 67% of actual recipients down in rank.
- The first-ranked candidate had an observed 6-week transplant-censored mortality of 15.7% under US-CRS versus 11.2% today, meaning sicker patients reach the top, and donor-to-candidate distance did not grow.

**Caveats.** Registry data and simulation, not a prospective policy trial. The authors project fewer waitlist deaths; they have not shown it. The score still has to pass OPTN review and public comment.

**For us.** If adopted, listing priority will come from labs plus the support actually running, not from the decision to place an IABP or Impella. Expect fewer devices placed for status and more conversations about which MCS strategy the physiology justifies, with anesthesiology at the table for those escalations.
editorTakeHome: Score uses 5 lab values plus durable LVAD, IABP, microaxial pump and advanced MCS; no hemodynamics, no exception requests
Time-dependent AUC for 6-week waitlist death 0.81 with US-CRS versus 0.69 for the current statuses
Reordering moved 67% of recipients down the list and put sicker candidates first without longer donor travel

posts.headline: FDA early alert: Philips Lumify apps can demand re-registration and block scanning; 4 deaths and 8 serious injuries
posts.summary: FDA flagged a software problem in all Philips Lumify handheld ultrasound systems: the iOS or Android app may stop recognizing a registered transducer and refuse to scan until it is re-registered over Wi-Fi or cellular, and the USB link can drop mid-exam.
takeHome: Use Lumify only where Wi-Fi or cellular is reliably available unless another ultrasound is immediately at hand
Reported harm clusters in prehospital and field use; a software fix is in development and the USB problem is still under investigation
Any Lumify used for resuscitation, line placement or quick TTE in the OR or ICU needs a backup imaging option
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Handheld probes have become the default for perioperative POCUS, and the Lumify is one of the most common. The failure here is not image quality but availability: the device can refuse to scan at the moment it is needed.

**What happened.** On 9 October 2026 the FDA posted an early alert covering all Lumify diagnostic ultrasound software versions on iOS (2.X, 5.0, 5.1.2, 5.1.3) and Android (1.X, 3.X, 4.X, 5.1, 5.1.1). Two problems are described. First, the app may fail to recognize a transducer that was already registered and prompt for re-registration without warning, just before use; scanning is blocked until registration completes, and registration needs Wi-Fi or cellular access. Second, the USB connection between the transducer cable and the tablet or phone can disconnect or become unstable during use. Philips has received reports of scans prevented in ambulances, aircraft and field settings where connectivity is limited.

**Harm.** As of 29 September 2026 Philips reported eight serious injuries and four deaths associated with the issue. The FDA notes that delayed diagnosis and treatment in prehospital settings could lead to serious injury or death.

**What Philips says to do.** A customer letter went out on 24 September 2026: use the system only where Wi-Fi or cellular is readily accessible unless a backup ultrasound is immediately available, keep backup imaging available, share the letter with all users and post it near affected units. A software update for the registration issue is in development; the connection problem is still being investigated.

**For us.** Hospitals have Wi-Fi, but not in every OR corner, MRI suite, helipad or elevator. Open the app and confirm the probe is recognized before the case rather than at the moment of a cannot-ventilate or a PEA arrest, and know where the cart-based machine is.

posts.headline: EACTS issues the first dedicated guidance on iatrogenic aortic dissection, with procedure-specific algorithms
posts.summary: A multidisciplinary EACTS expert consensus on aortic dissection caused by cannulation, clamping, catheter manipulation or device deployment, covering definitions, risk factors, prevention, early diagnosis, acute management and follow-up.
takeHome: Covers open cardiac surgery and catheter-based procedures; outcome depends on the setting and how fast the tear is recognized
Procedure-specific algorithms for rapid identification, containment, surgical or endovascular repair, or conservative care
The mechanisms it targets (cannulation, clamp, catheter, device) are the moments to have TEE on the aorta
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Iatrogenic aortic dissection is rare, but when it happens on bypass or in the cath lab it is one of the few true emergencies in which the anesthesiologist with the TEE probe is often the first person who can see it. Until now there was no dedicated guidance; management has been improvised from case series and from guidelines written for spontaneous type A dissection.

**What this is.** An EACTS expert consensus document, first author Maximilian Luehr with an international writing group and EACTS document reviewers, published online 7 October 2026 in the European Journal of Cardio-Thoracic Surgery alongside the Barcelona annual meeting. The authors describe it as the first dedicated multidisciplinary guidance on the problem.

**What it covers.**
- Definitions and a classification of iatrogenic dissection, which the authors note usually follows direct intimal injury during cannulation, cross-clamping, catheter manipulation or device deployment.
- Risk factors and prevention, early diagnosis, acute management pathways and post-discharge surveillance.
- Procedure-specific algorithms for rapid identification, containment, surgical or endovascular repair, and conservative management where appropriate.

**Caveats.** The evidence base is registries and observational reports, so most statements are expert opinion. The full recommendations sit behind the journal paywall; the abstract gives the structure, not the thresholds, so read the document itself before changing a protocol.

**For us.** The practical message is about timing and vigilance: the dissection happens at a predictable moment, and recognition speed drives outcome. Keeping the TEE on the descending and ascending aorta when arterial perfusion starts, at clamp placement and release, and during any wire or device work is cheap insurance, and the algorithms give the team a shared plan for what happens next.
authorLimitations: Evidence to guide management remains limited, largely derived from registries and observational reports, with substantial variation in diagnostic and therapeutic strategies
